Mr. Speaker, the three governments of the United Kingdom, United States and France have all agreed on a communique, and we have already indicated to this house, through a statement of the Prime Minister, our strong support for the objectives of that communique on which the three governments are agreed. It might be that there is a difference of approach as to how the objectives of that communique can be realized between the United States on the one hand and the United Kingdom and France on the other; but I hope that any possible difference of approach will not result in a difference of policy. I think it is essential from everybody's point of view who is interested in getting this problem solved peacefully that there should be unity between those three countries as to how it should be done.
So far as the supplementary part of the question is concerned, Mr. Speaker, we did indicate to the meeting in London that we would be willing, of course, to attend the proposed conference if we were invited. The criteria which were laid down by the three governments for an invitation to that conference were ones to which we did not take any exception, namely the signature of the Constantinople treaty, the importance to a country of its shipping going through the Suez and the importance of the canal to the trade of a country. As it happened, Canada did not fall within those criteria, and therefore we did not receive an invitation, nor, indeed, did any other western hemisphere country except the United States, nor did South Africa. We have no complaints about that at all; but we would, of course, have been quite willing to attend the conference if we had been invited, and we indicated that to the governments that were meeting in London at that time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to authorize the unemployment insurance commission with the approval of the governor general in council to make regulations providing for the extension of the act to persons engaged in fishing notwithstanding that they are not employees of other persons, and for including as an employer of a fisherman any person with whom the fisherman enters into contractual or other commercial relationship in respect of his occupation as a fisherman, and also to modify the provisions relating to the requalification requirements for certain subsequent benefit periods and to adjust the duration of regular and seasonal benefits accordingly.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution standing in my name now before the house is almost self-explanatory; consequently it will be possible for me to join with my three fellow members this morning in making my statement short.
First of all I would like to express my gratification at the understanding that had been reached entirely without my knowledge, which was announced by the leader of the house.
On May 16 last I stated in this house that we had been continuing our investigations to find out to what extent if any the Unemployment Insurance Act might apply to a reasonable number of individuals who were engaged in the fishing industry, many of whom are self-employed. I stated that even though it should be found that a plan could be formulated to provide coverage for fishermen generally it would take a good deal of time to work out anything like a practical detailed plan.
The government has now given consideration to the outline of a plan which the unemployment insurance commission believes can be worked out in detail in a practical manner. This plan would give a limited coverage under special regulations to persons whose main occupation is fishing. For most of those engaged in fishing only seasonal benefits could be made available. In order to bring such a scheme into operation it
Unemployment Insurance Act will be necessary to have an enabling amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide for collections of contributions from and on behalf of fishermen who are not employed for wages.
In view of the wide variety of ways in which the fishing industry is carried on in different parts of Canada, several months more will be required before it will be possible to announce a practical detailed plan. It is the expectation of the government that this plan can be worked out in time to permit contributions from fishermen to commence by the beginning of the next fiscal year, which is the most satisfactory date if the majority of fishermen are to be put in a position to make enough contributions to qualify for benefits before the end of that fiscal year. This resolution forecasts a short enabling amendment for the purpose I have mentioned.
As to the second part of the resolution, the other clauses in the bill which will follow this resolution propose to modify section 45 (2) and other related sections dealing with qualification for benefit. The present effect of the act is that persons who become unemployed and claim benefits every year have to acquire 30 weekly contributions every year in order to qualify. The proposal will allow these persons to requalify if they make 24 or more new contributions during the preceding year. This change would be accompanied by adjustments in the duration of benefits on such claims and also in the duration of seasonal benefits. It is expected that a substantial percentage of those who were unable last fall to requalify for ordinary benefits will be able to requalify under the modified conditions proposed in the bill which will follow this resolution.
I am informed by the Clerk of the House that if and when this resolution is passed copies of the bill in both languages will be available at the table.

speechtext:
There are just a few
things I should like to say at this time. The Unemployment Insurance Act was completely overhauled last year and the committee went into the revisions exhaustively, but I am sure that most of us did not realize that the new act would impose such restrictions upon employed workers. I am sure we were all caught by surprise. This year many workers have been disqualified because of the requirements of the new act and I still think that those disqualifications were due to the manner in which the regulations were interpreted. It is true that early this year the minister authorized his officials to revise their interpretation of the regulations to admit some of those who had previously been disqualified. Even then, if my memory serves me well, the revision only admitted some 6,000 out of some 90,000 that had been disqualified by reason of the new regulations.
Of course, we were promised that some new revision would be made by about May 15, but that was not found possible, and even with the re-interpretation of section 119 (b) we found that a great many persons in the past winter were unable to qualify for unemployment insurance. So we welcome a revision of section 45 (2), which it is hoped will achieve the result desired.
However, I trust that the minister, in watching the effects of this amendment, will not permit it to go so long this coming winter as to disqualify again a large number of persons who are applying for benefits. Last year it was a case of waiting to see how bad it was going to be before we did anything, and the net result was that those persons who were unable to qualify suffered for the whole winter. They never got on the list, with the exception of those few who were able to qualify after the interpretation of the regulations had been altered. So I hope that, even though the proposed amendment to 45 (2) now appears to cover most of those who might find themselves in difficulties, if and when a new season of seasonal unemployment hits us this coming winter, too much time will not elapse before the minister will take whatever steps are necessary if he finds that even this new amendment to 45 (2) does not produce the desired results.
Now I should like to say a few words with reference to the coverage for fishermen. Those of us who were in the committee last year followed the discussions there with great interest, and all of us, I am sure, were pleased at the interest that was taken by the Minister of Fisheries himself. I am sure that the present regulations that are being brought in are in part due to the keen interest that was taken by the Minister of Fisheries and also
[Mr Gregg.1

by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I am sure that their combined interest in the plight of the fishermen had much to do with persuading the government to institute coverage for these men.
Whilst I am not a fisherman myself, I have felt right along that these men required special treatment because of the very nature of the work in which they are employed. True it is that one of the great difficulties that faced the department was the difference in employment between those who operated on the west coast and those who operated on the east coast. I hope that the amendment to the act and the subsequent regulations, when they are brought down, will take care of this coverage, but I am a little disappointed that it is going to be so long before they go into effect. Coverage has been considered since last year definitely and prior to that, with representations from the groups concerned, and now it will be another year before contributions will be taken, and still another eight months or so before they will be able to benefit.
I have one major disappointment with regard to the bill that will be brought down, and that is that on this occasion when the minister had a golden opportunity to amend another portion of the act he did not take it. I refer to section 67 (1) (c) (iv) with respect to married women. I still believe as I did last year, and I tried to implement that belief with action, that this clause should be eradicated from the legislation. If we could have it stricken from the legislation then section 161 of the regulations would become unnecessary.
I should like to point out to the minister that women now constitute 23 per cent of the labour force and that 15 per cent of all married women are now in paid employment. These are the figures given by the director of the women's bureau of the Department of Labour during the course of the consideration of the estimates of the department. Those of us who have repeatedly asked that this clause be stricken from the act are hopeful, since the minister has not seen fit so far to listen to our pleas, that the studies of the women's bureau of his own department will eventually convince him, and I trust that time will not be in the too far distant future.
You have here a large body of employed persons who suffer discrimination under the act which is not suffered by any other group of workers. In my opinion it is all wrong. We have to remember that the unemployment insurance fund is supported by these workers. The funds, now approaching the $900 million mark, have been contributed by those workers who are covered by insurance and these

funds, which they contribute through weekly deductions from their pay, are not subject to tax exemption. Whether they are insured or whether they are not insured they contribute to the fund, in the first instance through their weekly contributions and the lack of tax exemption therefor, and in the second instance by the government portion which is paid in turn out of taxes collected from employed persons. On the other hand, the employers' contribution is eligible for tax exemption in the hands of the taxpayer. The government contribution, as I said a moment ago, is paid for out of taxes, moneys collected alike from workers and employers.
Because of this it seems to me that all workers have a very real interest in the fund which is being built up, and now, when we have 60 per cent of the labour force covered by unemployment insurance, when we have such a large number of women employees both married and single, I think it is high time that the minister took another view of this offending clause and listened to our pleas to have it removed from the act. We will wait until we see the bill, Mr. Chairman, to make any further comments, and we will follow the discussion with interest.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to anticipate any of the details of the bill that follow the resolution. The impression may have been created throughout the country that we are rushing this matter through the house at the last minute, but may I say that is not the case. This matter has been under discussion and consideration by the members of the estimates committee who looked at the minister's estimates as long ago as last April. At that time the minister was not quite clear as to what he could do with respect to amendments, particularly with regard to section 45 (2). The actuaries have been looking at the problem since that time up until a few days ago. The minister now has the necessary data to bring in a bill which is a compromise having in mind what I should like to see. But I think that after discussing this matter briefly with the minister a few days ago, as a member of the estimates committee, the amendment to section 45 (2) will at least considerably modify the situation that existed last winter. I am not going to comment on it now because this bill, I understand, is going before the industrial relations committee where the members of that committee will take a square look at the details of the bill and also point out to the minister any other adjustments we may think necessary in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
There is one thing that I believe the members of this house will have to hammer
Unemployment Insurance Act home to the people of this country and that is that the unemployment insurance fund is a trust fund which belongs to the workers of this country. It is not only the responsibility of the Department of Labour and the Civil Service Commission to protect that fund but it is the responsibility of organized labour, particularly outside of this house, to use that fund as a trust fund that belongs to them. Anyone who injures that fund in any way should be taken to task.
Now, with respect to the fishermen, I may say that so far as the members of the committee are concerned it is the unanimous opinion that the fishermen should be brought under the act. However, it is going to be rather a difficult administrative job. It is not going to be easy, not nearly as easy as it is for the organized labour forces. I do not think we want to create the illusion that the mere passage of this bill will bring benefits to the fishermen within five or six months. It is not going to be that easy because the task of getting them registered, centred in their proper offices, that kind of thing, is going to be difficult. I do not think we should have any illusion as to how rapidly that will be accomplished.
I am not going to say any more at this time, Mr. Chairman, but I did want to dispel the illusion that we were rushing things. We have been considering this matter continually since last April and I believe the members of the committee are unanimous in believing that what we have arrived at is not all that we would like to see but it is the best we can do under the circumstances. The Minister of Labour has been very cooperative in the matter and I join with the hon. member for Hamilton West in saying that with respect to settling the question of bringing in the fishermen, a large part of the credit should go to the Minister of Fisheries. I do not want the press outside to get the impression that the Minister of Fisheries and I are now tilting across the floor to bring about the kind of thing he suggested a few days ago.

speechtext: It will come.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext:
I do say that in all sincerity because I know the minister and his departmental officials worked very hard on it. I know that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration worked hard as well, but of course he has a motive in that a large part of his riding is a fishing area. He is working for his riding, and rightly so. He was interested in seeing this thing brought about. I expect I shall have something to say when the bill comes back after we have looked at the details. I might say that the

Unemployment Insurance Act married women's regulations are something that I used to call the bear trap, but I think in dealing with the subject a few days ago before the committee, the hon. member for Hamilton West will agree with me, there has been a modification in the administration and they certainly are not working the way they used to do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext: They should not be there at all, anyway.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext: The last time we amended the act, we took that out but the actuaries placed it back in. I do think there has been a modification with respect to administration, but I agree they should be out and that has been my main demand over the years. However, I am glad we arrived at this decision to get this matter finalized before the session closes. I will say that in my judgment the arrangements now made with respect to amending section 45 (2), by reducing the number of weeks to qualify from 30 to 24, will take care of the big load now. Officials of the unemployment insurance commission showed us, with the use of charts, how it would have worked week by week last year. I think that, if the data are correct, this is going to bring a lot of relief and will pretty well cure the situation that we faced last year with respect to seasonal unemployment. At the same time, it is not going to cover everybody and there will be difficulties with regard to qualifications. However, the amendment is going to break the back of the big load we encountered last winter.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext:
In speaking on behalf of this group, Mr. Chairman, I might say that we welcome the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Labour. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, section 45 (2) has been continually before the committee throughout the whole of the session, as well as other labour problems. The minister has been kind enough to frequently call the steering committee together to discuss certain phases of the question so we must say we have been kept thoroughly informed as to what we might expect will take place.
I am satisfied that if the regulations connected with section 45 (2) are as good as they were when we first revised the act two years ago, then in all likelihood they will meet the desires of the employees. In so far as the part having to do with the fishermen is concerned I, too, would like to be counted with those who have complimented the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration upon doing their best to bring this about. I know something of the interest the Minister of
[Mr. Gillis.J

Fisheries has taken in getting unemployment insurance for the fishermen, because we both have fishermen in our ridings on the Pacific coast. The hon. member for Fraser Valley has spoken of the need of fishermen for this provision, and he too has received representations from them. I am sure that they will welcome this part of the resolution, but I foresee a great deal of difficulty in the administration of the act. However, the fact the department realizes its responsibility is of considerable merit, and I would say we could probably leave it to the administration to work out the details.
I have not, therefore, very much more to say at this time since we have agreed that we should have only one spokesman from each group. I think we can do a great deal more of our study of this matter in the industrial relations committee. After we get the bill and study it in more detail, we will have more to say on it on second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING PROVISIONS TO PERSONS ENGAGED IN FISHING
speechtext:
I want to thank the three speakers for their co-operation this morning, Mr. Chairman, and I join with them in expressing gratitude to my colleagues the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for the part they have played in making this resolution with special reference to fishermen possible. These remarks apply also to the officials of the Department of Fisheries and the departments other than my own because this has been a joint departmental effort to reach this stage.
The hon. member for Hamilton West expressed some regret that there will be delay even yet with the insurance plan for fishermen. I think it very important, in taking this vital step, that we should do everything we can possibly do to make sure that when the plan does come into effect it will work as well as possible. We believe it may be necessary for some of our officials who have been working interdepartmentally on this to go to parts of our fishing areas to hold hearings or to investigate the conditions that exist there so that the plan might be tailored to take them into the best advantage. I do not mean taking in in the sense that is sometimes used, but to cover the fishermen to the best advantage.
Since the question has been asked, I might make the statement that the plan is intended to cover not only the fishermen on both coasts but also those engaged in commercial fishing in fresh water, not the kind with the rod and the fly.
The hon. member for Hamilton West hoped that too much time would not be lost in bringing it into effect. I can assure her that

we will not delay. She also asked us to watch the working of the amendment to section 45 (2) when we come into the fall of this year. We will do that, unquestionably. It should be recalled by the committee that every fall, as a matter of fact, every month of the year, a great many insured workers, whose applications cannot be accepted for a great variety of reasons, apply for insurance. Consequently, out of the 90,000 that were turned down last fall, there were a great many who would have been turned down had the act never been amended, last session.
With regard to the married women question, we shall continue to have that matter kept under study and very careful consideration. The hon. member for Cape Breton South said-and I was very glad to hear him say it-that we are not rushing this through parliament. The fishermen question has been before the officials of this government, the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Labour for five or six years. It has been intensively before us now for two years. Ever since last Christmas section 45(2) has been a source of concern, study and worry as far as my people are concerned; that is, on the official level. As far as the House of Commons is concerned, both items have been to the fore and have been carefully considered ever since the estimates committee met in the early days of March.
Furthermore, we do not want to create the illusion that by bringing in this enabling clause to the act, which will come in the amendment, the fishermen will be getting unemployment insurance next week, next month or even at the end of this year. It will take time for the plan to be completed. When we come to the committee of the whole I shall not be able to answer questions in detail on the plan because of the fact that I do not want to tie the hands of those who are now charged with the responsibility of completing the plan. I shall be able to give, as I have already given or as the resolution has given, certain broad principles governing it.
I think that covers the points that have been made, and I again say, sir, that the Clerk has on hand a supply of the bill for study so that the second reading can be moved forward.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the international wheat agreement opened for signature at Washington on May 14, 1956, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the international wheat agreement, which came into operation in 1949 and was renegotiated in 1953, expired at the end of July this year. In order to continue the agreement, the United Nations convened a conference which succeeded in renegotiating the agreement again, subject to signature and acceptance by the governments of the countries concerned, to run for an additional three years up to July 31, 1959. Thus it is anticipated that the agreement, which has completed seven years, will have at least 10 years of operation.
The results of the renegotiation were announced in the house on April 23, and to bring hon. members up to date on the developments since then, I should mention that the agreement was open for signature from May 14 to May 18, during which time the agreement was signed by the seven participating exporting countries and 34 of the importing countries which indicated their intention during the negotiations to participate in the new agreement.
Signatory countries were required by July 16 to deposit instrument of acceptance or give formal notice of their intention to do so not later than December 1, 1956. The following countries have met this requirement: Argentina, Australia, Canada, France, Sweden, the United States. Importers: Austria, Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Costa Rica, Denmark, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, Germany, Greece, Guatemala, India, Israel, Italy, Japan, Korea, Lebanon, Liberia, Mexico, Netherlands, Nicaragua, Norway, Panama, Peru, Philippines, Portugal, Switzerland, Union of South Africa, Vatican City, Yugoslavia.
Exporting countries accounting for more than two-thirds of the total guaranteed quantity as well as importing countries accounting for more than this amount have complied with the acceptance provisions of the agreement with the result that the agreement came into effect on August 1, 1956.

International Wheat Agreement
Twelve of the importing countries represented at the United Nations wheat conference did not sign or accept the agreement, namely, Ceylon, Colombia, Cuba, Haiti, Honduras, Indonesia, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Spain, Venezuela, Ireland and New Zealand. It is possible that some of these countries may wish to be admitted to the agreement by accession at a later date. Only one of the 12 countries, Ceylon, has declared since the conference that it does not intend to take part in the agreement.
As for the agreement itself, I think that all members of the house will be disappointed in the government of the United Kingdom's declaration early in the negotiations that they would not rejoin the agreement. Because the United Kingdom imports a much greater quantity of wheat than any other country, the agreement is denied the leadership of the United Kingdom on the import side at a time when their effective participation would be welcomed by other importing countries and by exporting countries alike. On the other hand, the United Kingdom officials have advised us that their market for wheat is open to us without let or hindrance of any sort and that they anticipate the British millers will continue to prefer our qualities of wheat as they have done in the past. In other words, they will continue to do business with us, whether they are inside or outside the agreement.
Although the United Kingdom continues to stand aloof from the agreement, Argentina and Sweden have joined, for the first time, the ranks of the exporting countries. Argentina's participation will create a liaison through the agreement with the other exporting countries as well as the importing countries. This marks a new departure in the grain marketing policy of the Argentine government which is welcomed by both exporting and importing countries.
It has been disappointing to see the reduction in the amount of the guaranteed quantities for some of the importing countries which have remained within the agreement. Because of the reductions in the quantities of these importing countries the major exporting countries including Canada have had to reduce their guaranteed quantities by roughly one third from the levels of the 1953 agreement. Canada's new guaranteed quantity will be in the neighbourhood of 100 million bushels, depending upon the actual acceptances of the agreement by the importing countries. Not only has the easier supply situation within the importing countries as well as within the exporting countries contributed to this decrease, but transactions entered into or in prospect by some of the importing
[Mr. Howe (Port Arthur).!
countries with the United States under the provisions of public law No. 480 have induced them to refrain from putting a high percentage of their total import requirements into their guaranteed quantities under the agreement. Such wheat transactions on noncommercial terms do not qualify for registration against the United States guaranteed quantities under the agreement and it is unfortunate that the existence of such transactions is operating to limit the present scope of the agreement.
When it became known to us that the guaranteed quantities would be reduced, our delegates to the conference were instructed to take a very firm position on prices because we were not prepared to make price concessions in return for such reduced quantities. In the end agreement was reached on a price range of $1.50 minimum-$2 maximum, which represents only a token reduction from the $1.55-$2.05 price range negotiated in the 1953 agreement.
As on other occasions, the government and our delegation had as advisers the presidents of the principal western farm organizations who all endorsed renewal of the agreement on the terms that have been agreed.
Although the agreement does not, as we might have wished, cover a major portion of the world trade in wheat, one must bear in mind that the background wheat position created a difficult atmosphere for the renegotiation of the agreement. Therefore, there is some reason for satisfaction that agreement could be reached on the present basis which will provide time not only for the supply situation to level out, but also to test the degree of continuing support for the agreement.
With a few notable exceptions, the great majority of importing countries have attached continuing value to their participation in the agreement. They have no reason to fear for lack of supplies of wheat in the immediate future, but they do value stability in agricultural prices to which the agreement has contributed. For our part, we attach value to the fact that forty nations or more have recorded their acceptance of a range of prices from $1.50 to $2 as a fair range for the course of wheat prices over the next three years.
The agreement also contributes to understanding and exchanges of views between the trade representatives of the importing countries and the exporting countries and to exchanges of views among the exporting countries in which Argentina and Sweden will now participate, as well as Canada, the United States, Australia and France.

These more intangible values might be regarded as the real substance of the agreement rather than the contractual guarantees which the agreement contains, namely, a market for 100 million bushels if offered at the floor price of $1.50. It is because so many countries are still prepared to subscribe to the principle of stability in the international level of wheat prices that I commend this new agreement to the house for approval.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having regard to the lateness of the session the viewpoint that will be expressed by the opposition through me will be limited very considerably.
The minister has mentioned the disappointment of the government in the fact that the amount of wheat that will be purchasable from Canada has been considerably reduced under wheat agreement No. 3, the amount of the reduction being some 50 per cent. Indeed, when the parliamentary assistant to the minister referred to the agreement on April 23 he made this statement in part as reported at page 3161 of Hansard for that date:
. . . notwithstanding inadequate quantities Canada should continue to participate provided there was no substantial reduction in maximum and minimum prices from those included in the present agreement.
There has been no serious change in either regard, the reduction being, as the minister says, five cents on the maximum and the same amount on the minimum.
It is of interest to note that in effect what has been done in respect of the amounts purchasable under this agreement is the establishment of a floor price for wheat. That is an important matter and achieves in part, although to a limited extent as compared to previous agreements, something that the farmer in this country and I think generally throughout the world does desire, a stabilizing security and a floor price.
However, it is also interesting to note that while the floor price is a little different from what it was when the first agreement was made farmers generally find their purchasing power has been materially reduced during the period of approximately seven years that the agreement has been in effect.
The reason for this is simply the fact that Canada's dollar is becoming more and more anaemic through inflation. The tendency is a downward purchasing power for the Canadian dollar. The problem of inflation, more and more serious as the days go by, is one that must be faced by Canadians.
I point out the difference in purchasing power over a given period of time. My 67509-448
International Wheat Agreement information is secured from the submission of the interprovincial farm union council in June and the figures given not having been challenged may be accepted as representative of the facts.
In 1948-49 the purchasing power per bushel, based on a comparison with the period from 1935 to 1939 being 100, was then 93 cents. It has gone down gradually since, year by year, until in 1950-51 the purchasing power was 86 cents; in 1951-52, 81 cents; in 1952-53 the same. Then there was a material diminution in 1953-54 to 70 cents, and in 1954-55 to 61 cents. The latest figure estimated for 1955-56 is 58 cents. In other words, while prices under the international wheat agreement have changed little in the intervening seven years they have been greatly altered in their effect by the reduced purchasing power of a bushel of wheat, falling as it has from 93 cents to 58 cents, a decline in purchasing power of 62 per cent.
As far as the agreement is concerned, it does achieve some measure of futher stability, although without the United Kingdom as a member it cannot be as effective as otherwise might be the case. The minister said that he was disappointed that the United Kingdom had not joined in the agreement, but he pointed out that the United Kingdom would still require to purchase large quantities of wheat. A little later I intend to make reference in that direction and to suggest to the government that measures be taken as between Canada and Great Britain to bring about a larger measure of trade than is the case today.
Too often we in Canada think only of our economic relationship with Great Britain. Too seldom in recent years has our attitude been to consider and to support the world leadership of Great Britain. That is particularly so at this moment when Great Britain finds herself in one of the most challenging situations in her history. Canada's attitude toward Great Britain as revealed again today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not that directness which would be expected under the circumstances. It is almost one of pussyfooting disregard of the serious situation which prevails in the Middle East. We think of our economic relationship but we should be thinking of our political and international relationship within the British commonwealth and be ready to take a stand in keeping with our responsibilities within the commonwealth.
As far as the wheat agreement is concerned, its purpose is, first, to secure greater stability of income of both producers and consumers of wheat and, second, to provide a mechanism for the orderly adjustment to

This agreement in no way meets the serious situation in which we find ourselves. Once more this year Canada is faced with vast surpluses, and this situation is true not only in Canada but throughout the world. According to the latest figures the supplies of wheat remaining on hand on about June 1 of this year in the four major exporting countries for export and carryover total 1,887 million bushels, or 1 per cent more than a year ago. In the case of the United States, the supplies on hand at June 1 amounted to 1,057 million bushels, a small increase over a year ago. Canada had almost 600 million bushels on hand, as compared with 541 million bushels at the same period last year. There has been some change in that figure, but not a material quantitative change. Australia had 160-8 million bushels as compared with 133-8 million bushels; and Argentina had 69-7 million bushels as compared with 143-8 million bushels a year ago.
We have once more in prospect a very large crop of wheat on the prairies. What is to be done about this situation creates one of the great problems facing us. I say that this problem will not be met by the present agreement representing, as it does, a market for only 100 million bushels of Canadian wheat.
What must be our purpose in international trade? After all, Canada is a trading nation, in particular agriculturally so, and it is to this I am directing my attention at the moment. Action will have to be taken through multilateral trade agreements and by cooperation among the free nations particularly if we are to avoid finding ourselves in a worsening position with surpluses ever piling up and with restrictions against importations in various parts of the world. The best summary on international trade I have found is that made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in its brief to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects on March 5, 1956, and I quote:
In arriving at the best possible international trade policies, it is necessary to recognize that from the farmers' point of view several basic aims and objectives must be taken into account, and given proper weight.


To give every encouragement to the freest possible inter-exchange of products between nations.
To maintain and increase Canada's position as a successful world trader-something upon which the whole Canadian economy depends.
To maintain and develop Canada's export markets for agricultural products-of which she is a surplus producer. This applies particularly to wheat and other grains, but also to meat, some dairy products and by-products, and some fruits and vegetables.
To protect the prices and incomes received by farmers from excessive decline.
To protect the land, and to develop technical and human resources that make up Canada's farm industry.
The brief proceeds in that way. As far as this agreement is concerned, it is merely one of the means that can be used, and further means will have to be adopted. Not only are our farmers finding themselves in the position of having ever-increasing surpluses of wheat on hand; with the exception of the last few weeks there has been a profound loss of wheat markets, in particular Great Britain, which was for many years our major market. The situation in Canadian agriculture is set out by the Canadian federation in its brief to the government on February 14. It says:
From the point of view of prices, farm products now show a price decline, taken as a whole, to about 20 per cent below a fair relationship level- whether this is calculated on the base period of 1925-29 used by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or the more recent period of 1943-45.
Farmers from coast to coast feel keenly that on the average their returns have become badly out of balance with those of other major economic groups in the nation. It is important to emphasize purchasing power in this connection because the farmer's difficulties are to be found as much in high prices of the things he buys as in a decline in the number of dollars he receives.
I am not going to go into details of the summary of the international wheat agreement that was made by Mr. Graham Spry in the summer 1956 issue of the International Journal, but this article clearly sets forth the very serious situation for wheat farmers generally. It says:
The importers, far more than the exporters, were determined to get an agreement and on February 27 took the exceptional course of stating publicly, in reply to the United Kingdom, that previous agreements "had promoted and maintained a degree of stability" and that they wished to negotiate a renewal . . .
In a situation of world surplus and possible collapse, the minimum price is more significant than the maximum. The adherence of two new exporters, Argentina, a major exporter, and Sweden, as well as the United States, Canada, Australia and France, members since 1949, greatly strengthens the floor or minimum price in world trade. These six are responsible for 90 per cent of world wheat and flour exports.
On that basis, this agreement at least represents a floor price in general for approximately one-third or more of the amount of

wheat Canada will export, and therefore is beneficial to that extent. What farmers will do. however, under this agreement, if the continued effect of inflation wipes out even more than today the purchasing power of their dollar, no one can foretell. Since the farmer's bushel of wheat purchases today only 40 per cent of what it did when this agreement was first brought into effect, and since the trend is in the direction of higher and higher prices for the things the farmer has to buy, this agreement at the end of three years may well represent a minimum price serious to the preservation and maintenance of the agricultural machine within our country.
Canada and Australia today are the only two exporters in the world that subsidize neither wheat prices to their farmers nor export prices to their buyers. That is the reason that wheat farmers find themselves in the serious position in which they are today.
I should like the minister to tell the house and the country something of what the export situation from Canada of wheat may be expected to be during the months ahead. There has been some increase in recent weeks and months, but in considerable measure that increase represented the filling up of the world demand during the period when there was a material decrease in exports of wheat from this country. What is the actual amount of the carryover as of the beginning of this crop year? What is the expected and estimated amount of the wheat crop this year? The minister might also tell the house and the country what is going to be done to increase our share of the world market- for certainly the United States has in the past two years, by the adoption of policies which in part are a denial of the principles of GATT, had a considerable effect on our diminishing wheat markets and reducing Canada's share.
On August 2 the department of agriculture of the United States reported that during the past year its increase in exports of farm products had been very considerable, and that, other than cotton, which had declined very seriously because of conditions in Egypt and in Asia, the United States increased its exports of all farm products by approximately 26 per cent over the previous year. In fact, this was due to the disposal program authorizing the sale of surpluses abroad for foreign currencies, those currencies being used for economic development in the countries designated.
During the past year, the United States has increased its grain exports by 33 per cent. That indicates that the United States is taking over markets that were ours previously, that we have failed to keep abreast of.
7057
International Wheat Agreement
This agreement in itself does represent something that is beneficial and is asked for by farmers everywhere in this country; but the wheat farmers of this country must not be allowed to have built for them optimistic expectations of markets being available during the coming year which were not open and available during the last year.
Finally, sir, I think that a great responsibility rests upon the free nations today to ensure that the surpluses which have been, built up will not be wasted. The dangerous situation in the Middle East today makes it necessary that the free world have available surpluses, should the terrible consequences of a failure of negotiation plunge that part of the world, and possibly the whole world, into war. To that end, more than ever before, I think the United States should be made to realize that we in Canada view with deep annoyance the type of policies that the United States is expanding whereby, in a give-away policy, demand for wheat generally, paid for on economic terms, is being undermined. Up to the present time the United States has shown little interest in the objections raised by Canada to the policy that is being followed by that country. The United States eats its cake and has it too. It remains within the international wheat agreement and at the same time, outside of the wheat agreement, acts in a manner that constitutes a denial of the basic principles upon which that agreement is founded and can operate.
Second, outside the agreement but within the limitations imposed thereby, I believe that Canada must to a greater extent than has been the case in the last two or three years endeavour to expand its wheat trade generally in the world. Last year Japan purchased, as I remember, some 16 million bushels of wheat from Canada. The Japanese are good traders and they have proven in the past to be good payers. In order to build up our wheat trade in Japan and in other countries that have similar qualities, I believe-that Canada, in order to preserve her international trade in wheat, will have to be prepared to make loans to such countries as Japan in order to provide the necessary funds so that Canadian wheat can be purchased by those countries.
Third, I ask the minister: What are the free nations doing to establish a food bank? Wheat does not deteriorate in storage to any serious extent. The international organization, F.A.O., has advocated such an instrument. It seems to me that a food bank cannot be secured under the United Nations. That being so, what consideration has been given to a food bank being set up by the.

International Wheat Agreement "North Atlantic Treaty Organization, representative as it is of the free nations joined to preserve freedom?
Next, I ask what is being done to increase *and expand our share of British trade. Mr. *James S. Duncan, former president of Massey

HaY'ris-Ferguson Limited, and now chairman of the dollar sterling trade council, set out in a recent issue of the Farmer's Advocate principles that I believe are necessary. He said:
Unless Canadians awake to the necessity of preserving and strengthening their historical and traditional markets with the United Kingdom and the sterling area by increasing imports from them, the outlook for the long term sale of some of our primary products is not at all bright.
He goes on to say that if encouragement were given in Canada to an increase of even 10 per cent in the amount of imports from the United Kingdom that increase would in large measure remove the serious adverse balance of trade between Canada and the United States and would place the United Kingdom in a position where it would be able to purchase a larger amount of Canadian farm products. He went on to say:
. . . we would not only ease our deficit with the United States but close the gap with Britain and enable it to buy more from us.
Would the minister say what is being done in that connection, for outside of the wheat agreement a very serious challenge faces the Canadian wheat farmer? What is being done to provide markets? Has any serious consideration been given to the establishment of a food bank? What attitude does the minister take towards loan advances to countries that require wheat, countries in which a larger measure of wheat trading can be expected in the years ahead, if at the present time a good trading relationship is established with them?
These are but one or two of the matters which in my opinion deserve the attention of the government. The hew wheat agreement, providing as it does for only 100 million bushels of wheat, merely touches the outward fringe of a problem which has worsened in recent years. What will be done by the government to provide expanding markets for Canadian wheat? What are the expectations for the next year? Have the nations of the free world learned yet the need of maintaining surpluses against the possibilities of dark days ahead? After all, this is not a problem peculiar to the western provinces but one that affects the economy of the dominion, for if the western wheat farmer does not receive a fair and proper price for his wheat and a reasonable assurance of markets detrimental effects will come to all parts of Canada in a reduced demand for industrial and other products.

Mr. Speaker, since the end of the war in 1945 Canada has been selling a substantial quantity of wheat under long term contracts and agreements with other nations. The policy of participating in the international wheat agreement has been supported, advocated and promoted over the years by the farm organizations representing the grain producers. I think the farm organizations in Canada are an outstanding example of a widespread organization that advocates a responsible policy, an organization that has assisted in a very important and material way in formulating national policies for the disposal of the products with which they are concerned. If there is one single reason more than any other why we are today considering an international wheat agreement it is perhaps because the farm organizations of Canada have consis^ntly supported an international wheat agreement. Whether or not the Minister of Trade and Commerce was right in February, when he suggested that unless some two-thirds of the world's wheat going into international trade were covered by a wheat agreement Canada should not be interested, only time will tell. The fact we have an agreement today covering a much smaller part of the world's trade in wheat being presented to this house for approval is mainly because the farm organizations have said they wanted an international wheat agreement, even though such international agreement might cover a relatively small part of the wheat going into international trade.
If one looks over the quantities of wheat that will be covered by this agreement and compares it to the other international wheat agreements in which we have participated in the past, one is almost forced to the conclusion that this agreement is not enough; that Canada will have to do some new thinking as to its wheat policy in the future; that governments throughout the world are going to have to bring forward some alternative to the policy now being followed. The reason is quite obvious. It is the fact that each successive wheat agreement that is signed covers a smaller and smaller part of international trade. The first international wheat agreement after the war covered 595 million bushels, and that was rather an effective agreement. The next agreement, the one just ended July 31 of this year, covered a much smaller quantity, 394 million bushels. The agreement today, if all listed countries had ratified, would cover an even smaller quantity, 302 million bushels. In his statement to the house the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that there are 12 of these nations that have not yet signed the

agreement and the 302 million bushels is based on the assumption that they would. So we have an agreement that may cover less than 250 million bushels of wheat.
Of that quantity Canada's share is much less than 102 million bushels because our quantity is reduced in proportion. I am not certain, in view of our experience in the past, that we are likely to sell or export even that smaller quantity under this agreement. I have the figures here for the sales of Canadian wheat under the international wheat agreement through July 13, 1956, a couple of weeks before the end of the agreement. I do not suppose anything very material happened in the last two weeks. The figures show that for 1955-56, that is to that date, out of a total guaranteed export quantity for Canada of 153 million bushels, we had then exported something less than 75 million bushels.

I want to point out to the minister that that expression is the expression of the international wheat agreement wheat council in their regular publication, and I agree with the minister that when they say, "guaranteed quantities (export countries)", that name should certainly be changed based on experience.
The agreement we have today is perhaps important in that it indicates there is still a substantial number of importing countries that are prepared to sign an agreement. It is perhaps well to remember that the agreement was brought about after a long period of very difficult negotiations. I think as it now stands it should be a clear indication to this government, and a clear indication to our farm organizations and to the world, we are going to have to adopt new and different measures in the future if we are to have stability in the marketing of grain in the international markets of the world. As the hon. member for Prince Albert pointed out in his own statement and in the statement of others, this is a guaranteed floor price of $1.50 per bushel. I want to point out that even as a guaranteed floor price it is not nearly as
International Wheat Agreement significant as one might hope. It is a guaranteed floor price for a relatively small quantity of wheat related to the international markets of the world.
If the Canadian government passed on any such reductions to the wheat producers so that all the Canadian wheat producers would get for their grain was $1.50 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern Fort William, less all the cost of storage, administration and so on, it would spell a price to our producers in this country of about $1.20 net. This could do nothing but bring great financial hardship to the whole economy of the three prairie provinces. This agreement is of value, but it will not do the job of providing stability. One of the main stumbling blocks has been the attitude of the United Kingdom. As the greatest purchaser of wheat in the world her absence from the agreement has made the agreement much less effective. From what I have read, and I have done considerable reading as to the negotiations, I have come to the conclusion that Great Britain did not just stand out of the agreement and say, "You people go ahead and negotiate an agreement." She took an active role, and has indeed for a number of years, in opposition to this type of agreement. She has not merely, and this is very serious, stayed out of the agreement, but she has hoped that, by so doing, it would result in no agreement at all being signed.
I think when we are talking about commonwealth relations and commonwealth problems, people in high places in the United Kingdom should review their attitude towards the international wheat agreement because if there is going to be some give and take in international policy this is the place where the United Kingdom can give a real lead to the world. I do not think the role of the Canadian government is completely without blame. It is one thing to sign an international wheat agreement; it is one thing to sign contracts for the sale of wheat as we have done with a great many countries, but another thing is necessary and that is to see that the potential importing nations have the currency with which to buy our grain. Trade is a twoway street; we have heard that said many times. So far as the Canadian government is concerned in relation to the wheat trade, just as in relation to many other matters, they seem to think that trade is a matter of exporting Canadian goods without paying very much attention to the question of importing goods from potential customers.
One of the best things the government has done in recent months is to sign contracts with iron curtain countries for the sale of substantial quantities of Canadian wheat. That has been a good move. But, if such contract sales are to be repeated in the future,

International Wheat Agreement if they are to be extended, then the government will have to consider making contract agreements for the purchase of goods produced in the countries that buy our wheat. If we say to the U.S.S.R., to Poland, to Czechoslovakia, and to the other countries that have purchased our wheat, we will sell you wheat, we will give you a good price but we will do little or nothing to buy the goods that you produce and wish to sell us, then the agreements that have recently been signed may indeed be the last.
We in this group have always advocated that the principle involved in an international agreement should be extended. We have never felt content with even the best international wheat agreement that the world has yet produced. We have said that the best type of agreement should be one within the United Nations itself, should be one to establish an international food pool to take care of surplus foods that are produced in certain countries so that those surpluses may be moved to the deficit countries.
While the Canadian government's attitude in relation to signing an international wheat agreement has generally been commendable, its attitude toward an international food pool, toward an international clearing house, has been indeed a bad one. The Canadian government, a government perhaps that should be more interested than any government in the world in establishing international control of food surpluses, has opposed on every occasion every United Nations move to establish an international world food pool, or an international commodity clearing house.
If we are to have stability in the sale of our grain in the future, the Canadian government's attitude toward a food pool must be changed. Somebody may say, well, of course, the falling off in the quantities under the international wheat agreement just shows that state trading, state management of exports to the world, cannot operate. I do not agree with that at all. If governments of the world were not taking some measure of control over the export and sale of grain we would have had a collapse in the market for wheat long ago. And if the grain officials of the United Kingdom, together with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company of this country, had had their way, we would have had the grain exchange opened for the sale of wheat in this country which, I am sure, a certain collapse in the price of wheat to perhaps less than $1 a bushel, and that, together with the Canadian Pacific Railway attack on the Crowsnest pass rates, if it had been successful, would have brought economic ruin to 200,000 wheat producers on the


prairies. We are glad that the United Kingdom has not been successful yet-neither has anyone else-in getting the futures market, the speculative market, re-opened in Canada for dealing in wheat, and we are also pleased that nothing has as yet been done to change the rates covered by the Crowsnest pass agreement.
One of the most satisfying influences in the wheat picture in the world today has been our own Canadian wheat board. The Canadian wheat board has had to operate within government policy. They have not been able, because of government policy, to compete with the type of policies that have been adopted in the United States; and yet, circumscribed as the Canadian wheat board has been, they have done, in my opinion, an excellent job on behalf of the wheat producers in the assembling, the storing, the marketing' and the handling of grain. >
Some say that a government body cannot be efficient. I will tell you how efficient the Canadian wheat board is. The Canadian wheat board is so efficient in its administration that it has been able to function on behalf of the wheat producers of western Canada at a cost of five-eighths of one cent per bushel per year. Perhaps that has been the best investment the Canadian wheat producers have yet made in so far as the return they have obtained on their investment is concerned. The wheat board, within Canada, has been able to transfer from the international wheat agreement, and from other wheat agreements, certain stability to the Canadian wheat producer.
I was interested in a statement made the other day by the deputy minister of trade and commerce, Mitchell Sharp, when I asked him in the agricultural committee whether he felt the fact that we have a central selling agency in Canada for wheat made it possible for Canada to sign contract sales with the iron curtain countries. His answer, if my memory serves me correctly, was that certainly the fact that we had the Canadian wheat board made it much easier for the government to undertake such policies in the sale of grain.
We can talk about markets, and markets are necessary. One problem that has yet to be overcome, outside of the fields of markets in this country, is to deal with the question of a fair price-cost relationship for the wheat producer. Some may think that the Canadian sales of wheat in the last year have gone up to the point where everything is well for the wheat producers and the marketing of grain. There has been a substantial increase in exports of Canadian wheat, from some 251 million bushels a year

ago to about 310 million bushels in the crop year just ended; but this has been brought about, I feel, not so much from action by this government as by our participation in a generally expanding world market for the sale of wheat. Our sales have gone up. So have the sales in the United States. The United States sales will increase from some 274 million bushels a year ago to an estimated 330 million bushels in the crop year just ended. Our sales have gone up a substantial amount, but the sales of the United States have gone up by an almost identical amount.
If we are to be consistent in our policies for the marketing of Canadian wheat, I suggest that the whole question of stability should not, and must not, be confined to the sale of wheat on the international wheat markets.	We must take the concept of
stability right back to the local marketing point. I want to say that within the policy that has been followed within Canada in the last year the concept of stability, as far as quotas at local marketing points are concerned, has been thrown out the window, and in the last year we have had introduced the very rankest kind of inequality in the marketing of grain.	The crop year that
ended on July 31 saw approximately 50 per cent of the marketing points in this country at the relatively low quota figure of five or six bushels per acre. Within the marketing of grain in Canada there has been great discrimination, and without reason. No justifiable reason has yet been given for that discrimination. It is true that grain must be called out where the grades and types are available; but no one can tell me that the types and grades of grain available for market are confined by nature to marketing points along the C.N.R. and the off-grades of grain are confined by nature along the C P R. The fact is that the C.P.R. company has made a mess of supplying and allocating box cars. Because of its failure to comply with the requests of the transport controller it has cost grain producers living along side its lines tens of thousands of dollars. It is probably correct to say that the average producer living alongside a Canadian Pacific Railway point in western Canada had a quota of from five hundred to one thousand bushels less than a wheat producer living alongside a Canadian' National Railways point. Certainly that figure is correct concerning farmers with farms of average or above average size.
I make a plea to the minister. The type of stability we consider when we are talking about an international wheat agreement must be extended so that stability is provided to the wheat producer in the marketing of his grain.
International Wheat Agreement
The second great need for stability is to stabilize the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat. Our economy is prosperous and people say at the moment our economy is booming. While the economy is booming, the wheat producer is afraid that unless something is done about his plight he may go broke. The price of grain has steadily been declining. The purchasing power of a bushel of wheat today is reported by experts to be less than it has been at any time in Canadian history with the exception of a two-year period in the early thirties. Therefore we need parity prices and the wheat producer says that as a first step in the realization of this we should have parity prices at least on the grain that is marketed in Canada. That is not adequate and it is not a complete parity concept but it would be a first step in that direction.
The next thing that is needed if we are to stabilize the grain economy is something that has been referred to so frequently in this house during this session that even I am convinced any statement on it would be out of order; but I want to say to the minister the issue dealt with this session for-such a long period of weeks is just as important now as it was at that time a few months ago. The whole question of providing advance payments to producers for grain stored on the farm must be dealt with by the government and this problem must be solved if the wheat producer is to share in the general prosperity of this nation.
We suggest further an extension of contracts for the sale of wheat to countries other than iron curtain countries wherever that may be feasible. We also suggest we should be prepared to sign reciprocal trade agreements for goods purchased in countries which buy our grain. The government should be prepared to accept local currency wherever it is possible and grant by that means the credit that may be necessary to make sales of wheat possible.
In spite of the fact that this type of policy has been condemned and pooh-poohed in this house in recent weeks, I repeat that there is a substantial place in the international market for the provision of free wheat to needy nations to overcome hunger and to help overcome serious malnutrition.
Finally we suggest to the government that it should change its policy from one of opposition to an international food pool to one of support for this measure under the United Nations as the best method to deal with the problem of food surpluses in the world.
