speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a general agreement among the parties in the house that each would put up only one speaker to deal with the agreement now before us. Because of that fact I am sure we all welcome the opportunity of getting the measure passed and approved by this parliament, not because we feel it is of less importance than other things by any means but there are good reasons I think why we should not get into a long protracted debate on agriculture at this time although I must say that that subject is of such importance as to warrant almost continuous consideration until the great problems now facing the farmers of Canada are much nearer to effective solution than they are at the present time.
I am sure that if it were not for the general agreement among the parties there would be quite a number of other hon. members who would like to speak. I can mention a few in my own group who would ordinarily take part in this debate. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has indicated that he would have liked to say something; the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) would certainly be taking part; as would the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smith), just to name a few, and others. I am sure the same would be true of the other parties. However, the agreement has been made and we are going to stay by it.
The international wheat agreement which we are now considering will provide only a minimum of stability of wheat prices in this country, and for that matter in the world. Year by year the international contract has become less a factor in helping to stabilize farm income. However, little as it may mean, little as the stability that it provides today may be, we do welcome it at least as one means of helping to prevent complete chaos in the world wheat markets which I am sure would have developed before now if it had not been for the international wheat arrangement.

As other speakers have indicated, we are disappointed that the United Kingdom has not seen fit to become a party to the agreement. Some are inclined to blame Great Britain for remaining outside the agreement and perhaps carrying on year by year in the hope that she will be able to buy her supplies at a lower price. When one is inclined to be critical of Great Britain I think he should realize that since the war Great Britain has been fighting an almost impossible battle for her economic life. Because of that fact we should not be too critical of her.
I am quite certain that if our attitude toward buying British-when I speak of "our attitude" I am speaking of the Canadian attitude-since the war had been somewhat different, Great Britain's attitude toward becoming a party to the international wheat agreement might have been different. In fact I am inclined to believe she would have joined in the agreement. If Canada had shown more inclination to transfer some of her purchases to the United Kingdom I think it would have encouraged Great Britain to feel somewhat obligated to become a party to the agreement, but we did not.
Our Canadian people have got into the habit of buying from the United States and as a consequence we have built up a large trade imbalance with that country and we have left unpurchased from the United Kingdom many of the things which Canadians would gladly have bought if they had known about them or if the pattern of thinking and economic action had been somewhat different. So let us not be too critical of Great Britain. But as I say, we are disappointed that she is not a party to the agreement.
At the same time we welcome the fact that Argentina has seen fit to become a party. As one of the great wheat suppliers of the world, the fact that she along with other great exporting nations are parties to this agreement will, it seems, go far toward stabilizing the market for wheat, at least within the realm of the international wheat agreement.
I am disappointed of course that there are twelve nations still remaining outside the wheat agreement. Those are twelve importing nations and their imports would have made a difference to Canada's possible quota. I do not intend to go into this aspect of the matter as enough has been said already by the two speakers who preceded me to indicate that Canada's so-called guaranteed quota under the agreement will not be realized unless those twelve nations do come in. That in itself is a somewhat serious and disappointing factor. However, there is nothing we can do at the moment to force them to come

in, and we would not force them to come in even if we could. But, every encouragement should be given those nations to become parties, and if there is anything Canada can do in that regard we ought to do it.
Since the agreement we are considering provides only a bare minimum of stability for wheat prices, this government and this country must take steps to provide a greater measure of stability if that is possible, and I think it is. I think the farmers of the country have a right to their share of the national income, which they are not getting today. There is a wide disparity between what could be considered their fair share and what they are actually getting in relation to the farm population of Canada and the proportion of the total population which that represents.
We feel that where the farmers are not masters of their own destinies, where they have to bear the major weight of government policy in respect to tariffs and that sort of thing, then there is a responsibility upon the government to see to it that conditions are laid down under which our farmers can receive their fair share of the national income. Until they do, industry cannot make the progress it ought to make in this country. It must be remembered that there is a definite relationship between the buying power of the farmers and the wellbeing of industrial workers. As a matter of fact I think studies in the past have shown that as long as there is a fair balance between farm cash income, on the one hand, and industrial wages and salaries, on the other, there will be buoyancy in our whole economy, a minimum of unemployment and a maximum of well-being on the part of the people. Just let those two things get out of balance, by reason of a decline in farm cash income, let us say, and almost at once there is a dislocation of our whole economy and the first to feel that are the industrial workers. Unemployment then becomes a problem in the country.
From the economic point of view, neglecting entirely humanitarian aspects, it seems to me that the government is bound to take whatever action it possibly can take to see to it that there is a stabilization of farm income. One of the most important factors in that is stabilized wheat prices.
There are those in eastern Canada who are apt to say, "The farmer can turn to the production of something else; if he is not satisfied with wheat prices let him convert to another form of farming." I would draw your attention to the fact that a great portion of western Canada is peculiarly adapted to the production of one crop, and that is grain.
International Wheat Agreement There are large areas in the country which would require a tremendous effort to turn to the production of anything else, and then there is no guarantee that that would be successful. Climatic conditions and soil both contribute to the success of the one crop.
If we can specialize in certain areas of our country in the production of grain to feed the people, not only of our country but of the world, that is the kind of thing we ought to do. Western Canada is best able to produce grain crops and it would be difficult to convert to other forms of agricultural production. Markets might be just as difficult to stabilize if a greater production of other commodities was encouraged. So I say that the government does have a responsibility to make a continuing and intensive study of this whole matter with the idea of introducing every possible means of stabilizing farm cash income. As I said, one of the major factors in doing so would be to stabilize the price of wheat.
That is one aspect of it. There is another aspect, which is this. During the war and for some years after the war, the farmers of western Canada did accept a lower price for their wheat and other grains than could have been expected if they had been free to market anywhere in the world and take what they could get. I do not think there is any question about that. It has been variously calculated that the farmers lost from $300 million to $500 million under the ceiling prices that were imposed upon them. They accepted those ceilings, but they accepted them on condition that the government would keep its promise, and the promise given by this government was that if the farmers would accept a lower price for their products during the war, the government would stand behind them after the war in stabilizing prices over a long period. I say that it was a definite promise; there is no question about that. One could cite the speech of the prime minister of Canada of the day, Mr. Mackenzie King, who made that promise in unequivocal terms. I say that the farmers have looked in vain for the fulfilment of that promise. They are justified in expecting that the government will see to it that everything is done to stabilize their prices.
What are some of the means by which they can stabilize grain prices? I think it has already been put before the house in different forms and at different times, but let me repeat briefly that I think there is a great virtue in the two-price system. Those of us who do not support it are missing one of the best bets so far as the stabilization of farm income is concerned.

International Wheat Agreement The two-price system can best de described by simply saying that it includes an internal price based upon parity and an external price based upon the best you can get by negotiation and what you can get under contracts such as the international wheat agreement or bilateral contracts such as have been made with Russia and other countries.
With regard to the question of internal parity, every bushel of wheat that is supplied by the farmers to the bakers and the other consumers of Canada ought in fairness to carry with it a parity price. There is no argument whatsoever that can change my mind about that point. A parity price means to me a price that bears a fair relationship to the price the farmers have to pay. There are those who say that that would necessitate perhaps government subsidies. What if it did? The government subsidizes industry in practically every form through the tariffs; it subsidizes labour through labour codes, unemployment insurance and other things. It seems to me that the forgotten man of this country is the farmer, who has to sell for what he can get and pay the cost of freight both ways, on what he sells and on what he buys.
I say that there is no real, valid argument against establishing a parity price for all of the farmers' wheat that is consumed in Canada. There are those, of course, who claim that if we should establish parity prices, and an internal parity price for wheat, we would be forcing the Canadian people to pay a higher price for bread. Let me examine that for just one moment. I doubt it very much. The price of wheat has a relatively small influence on the price of bread. Investigations made during recent months show that since 1945 and 1946 the price of bread has more than doubled in its average across Canada. The 24-ounce loaf now sells for an average of something like 21-2 cents in the major cities of Canada. That is something more than twice what it cost in 1946. At the same time, the farmer, since 1946, has received very little more for his wheat, and the bakers admit that what little increase there has been in the price of wheat is not reflected at all in the price of bread.
The major factors affecting the price of bread are the price of labour in the bakeries and in the mills, in the concerns that make up the paper and all the other things that go into the packaging and marketing of bread; the cost of marketing and the cost of transportation. Those are the things that affect the price of bread. If the farmers of Canada were to be guaranteed a parity price for their wheat internally, it would affect
IMr. Low.]

the price of bread very little, if any. Even if it did, I am satisfied that every Canadian citizen would be glad to take care of that small increase in the price of bread as a means of ensuring that the farm cash income is kept at an economic level, a level that will guarantee the farmer a fair return for his labour and a return on the investment he has in this country.
So I do not hesitate for one moment to agree with those who claim that the best way to start guaranteeing stabilization of price is to establish an internal parity price system for the farmer. It would be easy if the farmer had complete control of his own product and could keep it under his control and sell it under his own agencies. Then he could set his own price and perhaps could achieve his objective without government help. But the government of Canada has undertaken to market the farmers' wheat under the Canadian wheat board and, having done so, it seems to me it has a certain amount of responsibility to see to it that something is done to stabilize wheat prices for the farmer.
The second feature, as I said, of the two-price system is the best external price we can get by negotiation and contract. That is what we have been doing, of course. We have been accepting what we can best get in the external market. The international wheat agreement and contracts between nations do add somewhat to our ability to stabilize prices even externally, but there is one thing that we must do, and that is to give credit to the Canadian wheat board for whatever stability there has been in external marketing. I think it has done a good job and the farmers of western Canada appreciate the wheat board. They would not want to go back to the old open market system of marketing, with the dealing in futures and gambling that went on over the years. The farmer was the victim, and the farmers do not want to go back to it, generally speaking. There may be some who would like to see a change, but they are in the minority. So far as we in this corner of the house are concerned, we certainly go along with the farmers when they say, "Let us keep the wheat board and give it every support."
As I have said, the wheat board has contributed to whatever stability we have been able to achieve externally in the marketing of our wheat, so long as it has kept itself free from the imposition of government policy to the contrary. There have been times when that has happened, and the wheat board's work was made ineffective. As long as the government allows the wheat board to conduct its own affairs as it considers best, I am sure that it will continue to get along well as it

has in the past. We stand by that two-price system and we feel that it would not be any great task to adopt it as a policy, and particularly to see to it that the internal price structure, so far as farm products are concerned, is based on parity.
Another important thing that would contribute, I think, to the stabilization of wheat prices would be a realistic trade policy in which we would recognize this very important principle: Nations of the world which may want to buy our wheat can only do so if they can get Canadian dollars or Canadian credits with which to make the purchase. That is basic and fundamental. It is simple. Consequently, if we expect Britain, India or any other country to buy Canadian wheat we have got to be prepared to buy goods in those countries and supply them with the dollars with which they can make their purchases here. We have failed in that respect in the past, and somehow or other we have got into the frame of mind where we look upon American dollars as the only criterion.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON ON MAY 14, 1956
speechtext:
It is not my intention to take up too much of the time of the house, but I think perhaps a few words are indicated by the remarks that have been made on this resolution. In recommending the resolution the government believes it is making an important contribution to the well being of our western country. On the other hand, statements have been made here that I think rather overemphasize just what the agreement can do. It has been suggested that the agreement guarantees a minimum price for wheat. Well, that is hardly true. This year the sales registered under the international wheat agreement were less than 25 per cent of the total sales. We must remember that no one is obliged to purchase wheat under the international wheat agreement unless we offer wheat at the minimum, which last year would have meant offering No. 1 northern wheat at $1.55 per bushel and this year would mean offering No. 1 northern wheat at $1.50 per bushel. Well, I would not like to be pressed into the necessity of offering wheat at those prices with any belief that the member countries of the wheat agreement would take up the wheat. There are physical difficulties of storage in the way, among others; and therefore I have never been prepared to suggest that the wheat agreement is a guarantee of a minimum price. Perhaps it contributes to that end, but the guarantee simply is not there.
The great advantage it seems to me is that through the international wheat agreement the exporting countries and the importing countries are brought in to a meeting at frequent intervals to discuss the marketing
International Wheat Agreement of wheat, the price and the conditions under which exporting countries sell to importing; countries. I believe that is very valuable.. We have established the fact that importing and exporting countries believe that for the next three years a price range of from $1.50 to $2 is a reasonable price range and we are not likely to be pressed by any country to move either below the minimum or above the maximum. As a matter of fact, regardless of our situation that more wheat is sold outside of the agreement than within the agreement, we have been able to maintain remarkably stable prices for Canadian wheat. The present price is $1.75 in gold dollars and the only periods in which the price has been below $1.75 were periods when the Canadian dollar was selling at a substantial premium. On the other hand, the maximum price has not exceeded $2, even at times when wheat was in short supply. Therefore, we have maintained price stability over a number of years, and I think the wheat agreement has contributed greatly to that end.
In spite of the rather pessimistic statements about the condition of surplus that we have in this country, resulting from a series of crops unprecedented in size, we have been making progress towards reducing our surplus. The crop of 1954 was merely an average, perhaps a little less than an average crop, and in that year we reduced the carryover of wheat by something over 100 million bushels. The crop of 1955 was the third largest crop we ever grew, and during the past year we have disposed of just about the equivalent of that crop. The actual figures will not be known until the bureau of statistics brings in its report, but I would say that whereas the crop was about 500 million bushels the disappearance of the crop will just about equal that figure. Therefore over the past two crop years, one of which witnessed a normal crop and the second a bumper crop, we have reduced the carryover by about 100 million bushels.
This year should cause us no great concern about marketing problems. In spite of a slow start, and in spite of the pessimistic view that was taken of the situation just about a year ago by so many people, both in Canada and abroad, the crop year 1955-56 ended with a most gratifying record of sales, exports and farm deliveries. This has been the third largest wheat export year since the war years. In order to find a large year we must go back into the 1920's and I think the year 1928 was perhaps a larger export year. This would be certainly no worse than the fourth largest export year.

first four months of this year United Kingdom exports to Canada have increased by over 30 per cent to record levels, and that this appears to be a continuing trend.
It is often asked, why does the government not balance our trade with England? I point out to hon. members that Canada has a free economy. Every member of the opposition can buy where he likes. If he would like to buy in England it would help us greatly to balance our trade with England. The government does not control the flow of trade. It is a matter of individual preference, and I hope it always will be. It may not be if we get in great balance of payments difficulties. We have had occasion where we could not permit the flow to go unchecked. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SUCCESSION DUTIES ON PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES, TIME COUNTED FOR PENSION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any need for any extended remarks on this bill. There are certain things that should be asked about it in committee but I want to make one observation concerning it and that has to do with the position of the members of the force who have already retired.


I am not going to make these remarks at any great length but I do want to express the regret of hon. members on this side for the fact that when an opportunity presents itself, as it has in this bill when we are amending certain pension regulations, the government did not take the opportunity to increase the amount of pensions paid to those members of the force who have already retired.
I am not going to accuse the government of a lack of sympathy because I suspect they are just as human as we are, but I do accuse them of neglecting the opportunity which should be taken to make an adjustment in the pensions of those who have retired. A great number of these individuals whom I know are up against a great hardship at the present time.
When we think of the service those members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have given to this country in pioneering the west and enforcing law and order in the west, not by force of arms but by the force of personality, reputation and character, when we think of those very splendid men who have carried the tradition of this force throughout Canada and have in fact in very large part enhanced the reputation of Canada as a whole, and then realize the condition of poverty and the narrow financial circumstances in which they have to pass their last years, then I think we are justified in saying to the government that they are doing a very grave injustice to these retired members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in that they are not making a revision of the pension rates in respect to those who have retired.
I realize that the bill before us is concerned with pension revisions for those who are now in the force and who will retire in the future, but I hope it will not be more than one year from now, in the session to come, that the government will introduce legislation making an adjustment in the pension rates for those who have already retired. If the government will not do it, I assure them there will be a change of government and the new government will do it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am going to be quite brief in speaking on behalf of this group. For some inexplicable reason we find ourselves in support of the views expressed by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and think there is no necessity to lengthen this debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SUCCESSION DUTIES ON PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES, TIME COUNTED FOR PENSION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to say a word with regard to the views expressed by my friend

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act
the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton).
I think his words were very timely and proper.
I have known members of this force for a great many years and I have seen them in action since the days when they were the Northwest Mounted Police. My father commenced to teach school near Fort Carlton in 1903 when the memories of the rebellion were still very fresh in the minds of those who had served.
Very few, if any, of those who served in the rebellion are still living although I believe there are three or four. However, many of those pioneers were discharged in the period from 1900 to 1910. The amounts they receive as pension are not in keeping with the service those men gave in preserving for British America the western plains. I remember old Lieutenant Colonel Sam Donaldson, a former member of this house and one of those who made the trek in 1874; I remember also men like Sergeant Dorion and Sergeant Pook, both of whom served in the rebellion.
When things were dark these men served and, as the hon. member for Kamloops said, they maintained law and order to a degree that few of us realize today. They did it by force of personality, by the tradition that the force had built up and above all by the ability of that force to attract to it the finest young specimens of manhood not only from Canada but also from the United Kingdom and to a lesser extent from France.
These men have no way to press their views before parliament. I do think that in appreciation of what they did we should not put them in the position many of them are in today of living in a state of near destitution. There are not many of them left; the old guard of the Northwest Mounted Police is practically gone. The cost of raising the pensions of those who were discharged before the new act came into effect would not be great. They are not legion but they are representative of a tradition and a service that deserves the highest appreciation from the Canadian people.
I join with the hon. member for Kamloops in asking that at the next session of parliament the pensions of discharged veterans of the Northwest Mounted Police-I like to think of them as that; they were later called the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and finally the Royal Canadian Mounted Police- be brought up to a fair and reasonable level.
Secondly, I want to say a word for those who are serving today. There are many retirements at the end of 20 years' service because these men are able to command considerably more money in civil life than in
the service of this country. They realize that the state cannot compete with private industry. I submit that at the earliest possible date reconsideration must be given to raising the rates of pay of the members of this force. In the early days of Canada the police received 50 cents a day and certain allowances. We have gone far beyond that as the years have gone by, but the increase has not been in keeping with the responsibilities and the need for maintaining the force at its present high level. Commissioner Nicholson has come up through the ranks to his present high post and is one of those who represent the finest traditions of this force.
I do not often ask that expenditures be made by the government, but I do believe that if the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is to be able to maintain in the years ahead the great principles embodied in its motto there must be a fair and reasonable increase in the pay and allowances of those now serving. The result will be that in recruiting for this force the state will be able to mobilize the best men possible and will be able to keep the good men when their period of 20 years' service and the like is terminated. Those men will not be as subject to the magnetic attraction from outside forces.
I do not intend to say more as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police needs no special advocate. Knowing what they have done, knowing of the unequalled service they have given to Canada, I think we all appreciate their work.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to concur in what has been said by those hon. members who have spoken and to point out the absolute necessity for an increase in the pensions of these men. I should like to give the particulars of one case. A former member of the R.C.M.P. who is 66 years of age and who spent 25 years with the force is in receipt of a pension of $91.25, which incidentally will be discontinued at his death because there is no widow's pension. An amount of $7.65 is deducted in Ottawa for health insurance; his municipal taxes cost him $9 per month; he pays $10 per month for electricity and $4.41 for his telephone, or a total of $31.06. That leaves him exactly $60.19 per month to feed and clothe himself and his wife.
I think it is a sad state of affairs when a man who has served the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a force which has such a tremendous reputation not only here but all over the world, should be forced to live on such a miserly pension. Surely the service which this man and others like him have

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act given to this country entitles them to a larger income than their present pensions provide. I go along with those who have spoken already in asking the minister to consider the advisability of increasing these pensions in order to provide these men with at least a moderate living.

Listening to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) one would almost get the idea that my attitude toward the mounted police is that of a Simon Legree. The hon. member for Prince Albert has been a member of this house for a good many years and I am sure he can recall more than one occasion on which I have brought into the house measures to provide for increases in the pay and allowances and pensions of the mounted police, which I am glad to say no member of the opposition has ever opposed in any way.
By and large we have had increased pay and allowances for the mounted police on more than one occasion in recent years. I am not claiming any particular virtue on our part for doing that. We had to do it in order to get our enlistments. In other words, when we are in a state of great prosperity as we are at the present time the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as an employer must compete against other employers in the country and must provide pay and allowances which compare favourably with those paid by free enterprise.
With regard to the matter of pensions, I am sure that all hon. members who have preceded me in this debate realize that increasing mounted police pensions for those who have already retired is indissolubly bound up with the pension position of retired members of the civil service and the armed forces. The hon. member for Prince Albert has said that the number in the mounted police who would be affected would be quite small in relation to the civil service, but I am sure that if he approaches this matter with the slightest degree of realism he will know that it is quite impossible to raise the 

vested pensions of one group of the civil service already on pension as compared with another group.

So far as the Department of Justice is concerned, and so far as I as the minister in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police am concerned, I have no objection at all to occupying such a role of trail blazer; but the government as a whole and the Department of Finance may have different views in these matters.
I must say in all fairness that in their attitude towards both pensions and pay and allowances they have been, I think one can say, quite generous.
There is another factor in connection with the pension of the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That is that the work which they do is such that they have to be in the very best of condition mentally and physically. For that reason it is always the practice in all police forces to retire their members at a considerably earlier age than members of the civil service are retired. When they are thus retired, on a basis of actuarial equality with members of the civil service, they will not get as large a pension as the civil servants, but they will get it earlier in life when they retire.
In most cases there will follow a period of some considerable time during which they will be able to supplement that pension, or perhaps it would be better to say that that pension will supplement the not inconsiderable amount which they will be able to earn from their own efforts. We have had many cases in which police forces of this country have been very glad indeed to take on as their chiefs of police high ranking members of the R.C.M.P. For example, if I am not mistaken, the chief of police of Edmonton at the present time and the chief of police of Vancouver are former Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers who have been retired by us and are on our pension. They are

obtaining from these other services a salary, I am sure, greatly in excess of our pension. When each retires from his present employment, he will receive two pensions, one from us and one presumably from the force to which he has gone.
Apart from these points that have been raised, I am sure that the purposes of this bill and the explanatory notes are so clear that for me to spend any more time on them would be to take up to no purpose the time of the committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EQUAL PAY TO FEMALE EMPLOYEES FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 445, to promote equal pay for female employees.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am just going to say a few words on second reading of the bill. It will be noted that the bill applies to all the "works, businesses and undertakings" considered to be within the jurisdiction of parliament, without exception, including crown companies. It will not apply to the civil service because parliament has already legislated in the Civil Service Act on that matter.
The bill provides that an employer is not to employ a woman at a rate of pay less than he pays a man for identical or substantially identical work, and it is the "job, duties or services the employees are called upon to perform" that are to be looked at to determine whether the work is identical or substantially identical. However, if in the case of a difference in the rates paid a woman and a man for identical or substantially identical work the employer can show that the difference is due to a general rule of personnel practice on such a matter as length of service 

or seniority, which he applies to all his employees regardless of sex, this is not a failure to comply with the act. The bill protects an employee who makes a complaint under the act from discharge or other kinds of discrimination on account of her action in making complaint.
The rest of the bill has to do with enforcement. I might outline how I visualize complaints may be dealt with under this proposed legislation. The bill provides that a woman who considers that she has a grievance under the act may make a complaint in writing to the Minister of Labour. The complaint will be investigated by a fair wage officer of the department who will endeavour to help the parties to a clear understanding of their position under the act, which may result in settlement either through withdrawal of the complaint or an adjustment in the wage rate. This stage in the procedure is to provide an opportunity for voluntary adjustment.
If a settlement is not reached the fair wage officer will make a report to the minister setting out the facts and his recommendations. If the complaint has merit, the minister will appoint a referee who will make a full inquiry, hear the representations of both parties, decide whether there has been a failure to comply with the act and make any order necessary. The order may require an adjustment in pay for as far back as the six months preceding the date of the complaint. Failure to comply with the order is an offence under the act.
This administrative procedure for dealing with complaints does not hinder an aggrieved person from initiating proceedings in court if she prefers to do that at any point up to the appointment of a referee. If an employer is convicted for failure to comply with the act, the convicting court may order the payment of the wages due the employee, in addition to any other penalty.
What I am about to say will answer the question raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) at a former stage. Where an employer is bound by a collective agreement that contains an equal pay provision substantially to the same effect as in the bill, grievances are to be dealt with according to the machinery provided in the agreement and not through the complaint procedure or court action which I have described. This is to encourage the parties to collective bargaining to take the responsibility for applying the equal pay principles themselves if they wish to do so.

On two
previous occasions I voted against bills introduced by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) which were, in many ways, similar to the one now before the house. I feel therefore that I owe hon. members and my constituents an explanation of my position with respect to this legislation. At first sight this bill appears to be quite simple and straightforward. Actually it involves factors which go to the very root of our present concept of work and labour, which in turn form the basis of our present wage and salary structure. In my opinion these factors deserve more consideration than they are likely to receive at this stage of the session, and for that reason I would have preferred to have this legislation left over until next session.
The purpose of the bill is quite simple. It is to eliminate discrimination as between male and female employees with respect to pay when employed on the same or similar jobs. With that purpose I am fully in accord. No one could be more opposed to discrimination of any kind or in any form than I am. But it does not necessarily follow that all such differences in pay are due to discrimination. In some cases it may be due to economic factors, such as the more rapid turnover of female personnel as compared to male personnel. Airline stewardesses afford a good example of this.
Cases where pay differences are due to economic factors are not examples of discrimination. I think we should be clear on that point. But in those very cases where pay differences are due to economic factors, this legislation will tend to cause discrimination because, since the pay will be the same, it will obviously be in the employer's interest to employ men in preference to women.
This is one of the reasons I voted against the bills introduced by the hon. member for Hamilton West. But apart from that, I am not at all convinced that this legislation is necessary. The only employees it will affect are those under federal labour laws. They are mainly civil servants, employees of crown corporations and employees of companies with federal contracts. It has already been pointed out that it will not affect civil servants, because a policy of equal pay for similar work already applies to civil servants. If the civil service can initiate such a policy without this legislation, why is it that crown corporations cannot do the same thing? Certainly we have it within our power to write this policy into a clause in our federal contracts.
A third reason I voted against the earlier bills can be found in the New Testament, in the 20th chapter of Matthew, to be exact.

It is the story of a man who went out at different hours of the day and hired labourers for his vineyard. With the first ones he hired he made a definite contract for an agreed wage for the day's work. With the others there was no definite contract and no specified wage agreement. The employer merely said he would pay them what was right, and they went to work on that basis. At the end of the day they all received the same pay. The first ones were disappointed because, having worked longer, they expected more.
Whatever lessons can be drawn from this story, no one can say that it teaches equal pay for equal work. Actually those labourers received equal pay for unequal work. I think hon. members will agree that the New Testament contains a great deal of wisdom, much of it far beyond human thinking, and when we embark on a course that appears to be contrary to its teaching I feel it is wise to pause and take a second look. I believe there is much more to this story than its emphasis on the binding nature of a contract. I think it rejects the purely materialistic concept of human labour, and implies that other factors besides time and output should be taken into consideration with respect to wage and salary scales.
I am not going to take the time of the house now to develop these points further, but I hope there will be an opportunity to do so at another session. There are other questions in my mind, such as what would be the impact on the fresh fish processing industry in my province if this legislation were universally adopted.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope I have made it clear that I am not opposed, and have never been opposed, to the principle of equal pay for equal work for women. I appreciate the problem, but I believe that a better solution can be found by revising the basis of our present wage and salary structure.
I do not intend to vote against this bill. All parties have declared themselves in favour of it, and it is not for me to take the attitude that I am right and the world is wrong. But actually it is not important who is right. The important thing, in my opinion, is that we are seeking together to find out what is right. On the other hand, for the reasons I have just stated, it would not be honest for me to lead anyone to think that I have suddenly reversed myself and developed an enthusiasm for legislation which I voted against in good faith on two earlier occasions.

Clause 4 is the first of several clauses in this bill which hinge on the legislation recently passed by the house in relation to the fiscal arrangements with the provincial governments. Where there is to be a provincial corporation tax or personal income tax as well as that levied by the federal government there must of course be provision for deduction in the case of such taxpayers. The question that must always be asked is, how much. Our position in this respect was, I think, made abundantly clear in the debate on that measure, which passed this house a fortnight ago. We do not think, under all the circumstances, that the amounts which are permitted to be deducted in such cases, as set forth in that legislation, are adequate.
Bill No. 418 is simply a companion measure which sets up the actual provision for deduction in such cases. I am saying this now, Mr. Chairman, to put our position again on record and to avoid repetition. What we had to say on the other measure stands. We accept, of course, the principle that the taxpayers in such provinces should be entitled to make the deduction rather than be faced with double taxation; but we repeat what we said then, namely that the percentages allowed to be deducted in such cases are inadequate. Those percentages are now carried into the provisions of section 4, and a couple of sections which follow, of the bill.

Income Tax Act

speechtext: It is a payment made, Mr. Chairman, during the first year of the residence in Canada of the immigrant family. Perhaps I can explain to the hon. member. I made an announcement one day, possibly when she was not here, that from July 1 onward it was proposed to pay to children of immigrants who came into the country until, under the Family Allowances Act, which is one year, they were eligible for family allowances, $60 a year, or a fraction thereof. Does it come under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration?
It is paid through my department.

May I say to the Minister of Finance what I said to the Minister of National Health and Welfare when we were discussing his estimates, that there is still some confusion in the minds of people who come into this country with reference to their status for tax purposes in respect of family allowances. I believe that when these people come into the country at the present time the Department of Citizenship and Immigration supplies them with a pamphlet or some sort of document which outlines to them precisely what their rights are taxwise in respect of their children with or without family allowances.
I have had two letters from and one conversation with persons who came into the country and were given no such information and who, because of that, were forced to pay. The time had elapsed when their assessments came back to them in which they could have made restitution of the one or two months, as the case may be, of family allowances which they received in the one year in which the children became eligible. Consequently they lost the benefit of the tax computation in that regard. One of those gentlemen told me that had anyone given

him such information at the time he entered the country he would have known how to handle the matter, but no one had done so. Does the Department of Citizenship and Immigration make sure that everyone who comes in now is given the benefit of this information?

We do the very best we can. I am sure hon. members will be glad to welcome the addition of oxygen to the group of medicines, the other four having been in the act for some time, which may be included within allowable medical expenses under section 27 of the act. It does draw attention to what some of us argued when the present provisions in this respect were introduced, that the list of drugs is not large enough, and I think the time has come to submit this to the minister and the committee for some future review.
This particular amendment arises out of the decision of the income tax appeal board last December when a gentleman by the name of Anatole Brunet of Verdun had sought to deduct from his 1954 income the sum of $742 expended by him on oxygen treatments for his wife who had pulmonary tuberculosis. Testimony of the doctors was that constant medical use of oxygen was needed to bring her relief and to prolong her life, but it was held that this was not a permissible deduction; it was not one of the things that could be included within the scope of allowable medical expenses.
It is unfortunate that the amendment does not make any retroactive provision. In taxation legislation we always oppose retroactive legislation where any burdens are imposed. Where the provisions are remedial there is no reason why, unless some discrimination were thereby created, legislation should not be made retroactive.
I raise the point, first of all, that there is strong reason for making the provision retroactive when one sees as striking an example as was raised in this case. This man will derive no benefit for this heavy expenditure made by him in 1954, or 1955, if he did make a similar expenditure in 1955.
The second point I make is that while an example has arisen now underlining in a very

striking way the strength of the case for the inclusion of oxygen within the scope of these medical expenses, there must be many other medical items deserving of inclusion. There are many drugs that are required by persons who are chronic sufferers from some ailments for which the case is just as strong as it is for insulin, cortisone, ACTH, oxygen and liver extract.
I realize that in the first instance this is a matter for the Department of National Health and Welfare, but when recommendations are made from that department to the Minister of Finance I am sure they must then become his responsibility as to whether they are to be the subject of amendments to the Income Tax Act that he is prepared to father in the house.
I do not know whether or not this study is being made at the present time in the Department of National Health and Welfare, but I do urge very strongly that such a study should be made by the proper government department, because I am satisfied that the present list is not adequate and that there are many chronic sufferers in this country who have just as strong a case for including within the scope of allowable medical expenses the substantial outlays they are making for drugs to alleviate their sickness as the case which exists for insulin, cortisone, ACTH, oxygen and liver extract.
While there is only one addition being made to the list this year I would suggest that there must be many others, and they should be diligently inquired into and legislation ought to be brought forward to enlarge this list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this amendment is to provide something different from what my hon. friend has in mind. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I do not see any advantage in this particular amendment. I have had a situation brought to my attention a number of times and I wonder if the minister is also aware of it. Frequently farmers have made money in two or three years and have filed returns and paid their taxes; then in a year when they have had a loss, through neglect or as a result of not knowing the terms of the act tney have perhaps failed to file a return. The history of farming is such that we all know in some years a farmer may make a great deal of money and in other years he may incur substantial losses.
What is to be gained by requiring the farmer to file a return every year even in the years when he has had a loss, in order to take advantage of the averaging? It would seem to me that within a five-year period, if the farmer has filed a return when he has had a taxable income, that he should then have fully met the law and should be able to average over the five years despite the fact that inadvertently he failed to file a return when he was not subject to tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The purpose, of course, is to be helpful to the administration of the tax laws of Canada and at the same time not to be harmful to the farmer.
My hon. friend would understand that if the farmer is not taxable in the fifth year, let us say, and then in the sixth or seventh year

Income Tax Act
he becomes taxable and flies a return and discovers at that time in the course of going over his returns that he was in fact taxable during the fifth year, he has lost an opportunity to elect back. In this way we can keep him up to date and he is able to take advantage of the averaging.
If in the seventh or eighth year he were to discover he was taxable in the fifth year it would be very difficult for him to average back in view of the lapse of time. This is not intended to be restrictive on the farmer; rather it is intended to be helpful to him to keep his tax returns up to date in order that he can take the full advantage of the law.
My hon. friend says we know that farmers are not aware of the law. There are some who are not, of course, but most of those who are familiar with income tax realize the advantage of averaging, and this is to assist them in making sure they are able to average for the five-year period.

Mr. Chairman, the point I wish to raise relates more perhaps to the realm of the administration of the act than to the actual clause. I had a very unfortunate case brought to my attention recently. One of my own constituents previously operated a farm in the province of Alberta and built up a dairy herd there. In 1953 he sold his herd, moved to British Columbia, and started up in the dairy business in that province.
This man filled in the forms in which he elected to average and made arrangements with a particular individual in the city of Chilliwack whom he understood to be dependable, and paid him a fee for filling in his income tax forms. Apparently the forms were filled in on time but through some circumstance which was beyond the control of the gentleman in question the forms were not received by the income tax office until approximately the 17th of the month, I think it was. Because of that unfortunate circumstance this man's request for averaging was disallowed and the result was that he was assessed a little over $1,000 in the form of income tax whereas if the forms had been filed on time the whole matter would have been taken care of and he would have been saved that amount.
Perhaps the problem lies in the administration. I realize there has to be a cut-off date, but this particular man had the receipt indicating that he had paid his fee and that the forms were being filled out. Because the man whom he had engaged to fill out his income tax return was lax, the return was not received in time and his client was penalized.
I took this up with the Department of National Revenue, taxation division, and also

with the Minister of National Revenue, but apparently nothing could be done under the circumstances. Although this is the law it is unfortunate that something could not be done in a case like this. 1 do not know whether any comment is necessary by the minister, but I suggest that something be done to take care of cases like this.
Clause agreed to.

I just wanted to ask a question with reference to this definition of farm property and depreciation. It will be recalled that a few years ago the matter of cutting timber on a farm was being considered. A good many farmers in my province and other provinces cut timber perhaps after 25 or 30 years. Income Tax Act
if a farmer cuts timber annually for sale, it is considered income.

As a matter of fact I think it is a matter that should be looked into very carefully. The explanation of the minister is that if a man cut the annual growth every year that would be considered income. However, if he cuts every 25 or 30 years that man's farm has been depleted in value to that extent, and it certainly should not be considered as income for that particular year.

speechtext:
As to
the contents of the bill, I think it may be said that we are generally in agreement with them; but we regret that the views expressed at the resolution stage of this measure by the Leader of the Opposition have not been given effect in the terms of the bill that we now have before us.
When speaking on July 2, as will be found at page 5579 and following of Hansard, the Leader of the Opposition urged that the bill when introduced should take account of the plight of those former members of the civil service and retired personnel of the armed services whose pensions, in the light of the depreciation of the dollar and the consequent diminution in the purchasing value of their pensions, now require action on the part of parliament. Redress is needed in the case of those deserving persons whose pension provisions at the hand of parliament have become quite inadequate in the light of changing events.
At that time the Leader of the Opposition drew attention to the forward steps that have been taken in both Great Britain and in the United States to deal with similar situations. He pointed out that, apparently with the concurrence of all political parties in Great Britain, legislative steps have been taken within the past year. He quoted what was said in the British House of Commons recently, in these words:
What we have to do is to take into account a total body of about 600,000 pensioners, who have retired after different kinds of services, with different kinds of pension, at different times over the past 30 years and more. What matters is to do justice, as far as possible, among all those individuals. One has to discard the idea of a simple, new scheme as soon as one discovers that whatever scheme of that kind one can devise, it will do justice that is too rough to be called justice at all.
Sir, that seems to be the situation here. Since many of these good people retired the value of the pensions to which they became entitled on retirement has depreciated, in many cases to the extent of 50 per cent or even more. It may be that in the case of some of those who have been retired now for a time they have become entitled to the old ugc pension, but then so has everybody else who has reached 70 years of age. There is no answer to the claim for equity on the part of those many people who have served this country well.
One must express a keen sense of regret that the plea made by the Leader of the Opposition for these worthy people has apparently fallen upon deaf ears. The Minister of Finance did not choose to participate in the debate at the resolution stage or to
make any comment on the plea that was made by the Leader of the Opposition in very earnest terms on behalf of these worthy people.
I do not know how many members of the house are aware of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that any retired civil servant who receives a pension of $1,200 per annum or more is not permitted to take on even part-time or casual work for the government without having the sum so earned deducted from his pension. Take the case of a retired civil servant who has not enough to live on and who may, for example, obtain a few days' work at some exhibition under federal auspices or something of that kind to make a little money to eke out an inadequate pension. Under existing government regulations, if his pension amounts to $1,200 or more he cannot take that employment, or if he does the amount so earned will be deducted from his pension. It strikes me that is a very striking form of injustice, an inadequate pension to begin with and then the deprivation of an opportunity to earn a few more dollars through casual employment by the government. Many of these people are in a position otherwise to be of service in such situations of casual employment.
I do not intend to enlarge on these remarks, except to express again very keen regret that the minister has not grasped the opportunity afforded to him to insert in the bill some provision to meet the needs of persons in the group to which I have made reference. So far as the contents of the bill are concerned, we are in general agreement with them, but we deplore the omission from the bill of any provision to meet the needs of a very worthy group of people who have served this country well in a variety of capacities.

Mr. Chairman, during the discussion at the resolution stage I raised a point having to do with section 13, subsection 4, of the act which deals with the amount of pension payable to a widow if she is more than 20 years younger than her husband. It reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, the amount of any annual allowance to which the widow of a contributor may be entitled under this act shall, if the age of the contributor exceeded that of his widow by 20 or more years, be reduced by an amount determined in accordance with the regulations.
There has been no amendment included in the bill to deal with that point, and I would urge upon the minister that he give consideration to modifying those regulations. This problem has come to my attention with respect to the case of a woman who had been married for 25 years, I believe, at the time her husband died. She is about 60 years of age and unable to go out and earn anything for herself. This matter was dealt with, of course, originally in the minister's budget speech, and again at page 3744 of Hansard of May 9 at the resolution stage. I do not think there is anything further to be said on it at the moment.

I have a word or two to say on this bill. It concerns the fruit and vegetable industry of British Columbia. It is very much regretted by our potato industry that the action recommended with respect to tariff protection against the importation and dumping of United States potatoes has not been taken. The minister said he would make a statement on that on his estimates. I am not going to elaborate on that. I regret it has not been done in this bill.
I thought that when the estimates came around it would be too late to take remedial action this year. In the light of the situation that our potato growers face, it is a matter for great regret and criticism of the government for its failure to deal with the situation.
Where?

So the reduction in price for that month is in the area somewhere around 40 per cent below the average; in fact it is nearly 50 per cent; it is somewhere between 40 per cent and 50 per cent below the average price. If that does not constitute dumping within the wording of our various statutes, then I think it is high time the statutes were amended so that effective antidumping action could be taken.
The report continues that this representative, Mr. Burrows, the secretary of the council, met with Mr. Plumptre and Mr. Glass of the Department of Finance, and Dr. Richards, Mr. Pearsall and Mr. Abel of the Department of Agriculture, all of whom said the same thing that had been said the previous day by the minister and the officials of the Department of National Revenue, namely that no remedial action could be taken under the Canadian legislation. This was the situation with which our apricot growers were faced last year, and so far as they can tell they are faced with very much the same situation this year.
I have been asked by the policy committee of the Penticton Conservative association to lay before the committee and the minister their recommendations with regard to tariff policy and action that has to be taken to protect the fruit-growing industry of that area, as follows:
The policy committee of the Penticton Progressive Conservative association through research has found the following:
(a)	The Okanagan fruit industry like many other agricultural centres throughout the country is going through a state of serious recession;
(b)	The situation is serious as many growers now have to look for outside employment.
I think I detected some laughter from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who we understood today was happy that some of his recommendations with regard to the situation of his fishermen had finally resulted in effective action being taken by the government. I think it ill-behooves any minister of this or any other government to laugh at a serious submission made by the fruit growers of any province, or of any area in Canada. I hoped that the minister, instead of laughing, would listen to what is being said and appreciate the fact that these people are facing a really serious situation, and might therefore do what he could to have his colleagues take effective action with regard to that situation.
Mr. Chairman, if I hurt the hon. gentleman's feelings I apologize.
It is not his feelings; it is the fruit growers you are insulting.

The Minister of Citizenship
and Immigration gives himself credit for more effectiveness than he has. It would take more than his laughter to hurt my feelings; but what I am seeking to point out to the committee and to the country is that when we bring up a serious situation it ill-behooves members of the government to laugh in a facetious way at the plight that faces any segment of the Canadian population. It is not my feelings I am worried about. If the minister has not the common sense to be concerned about his own feelings, then I shall leave it to others to deal with him. The submission continues:
(c)	The fruit growers themselves have attempted to improve their own lot but it is felt that the main help should come from the federal government.
Of course I should pause here to say that the only effective help that can come to deal with this situation is through action under the anti-dumping provisions under the tariff legislation. The submission continues:
On the basis of the preceding paragraph our committee feels that tariff protection and more realistic anti-dumping laws should be passed by the federal government.
We would therefore suggest that:
(a)	New tariff legislation along the lines as set out by the tariff committee of the British Columbia fruit growers' association be set up.
(b)	Anti-dumping laws should be revised in order to protect the Canadian fruit grower.
(c)	With regard to the question of the antidumping laws, an example of this is contained in the British Columbia fruit growers' association brief on apricots, which brief is dated August 6, 1955.
There, of course, they refer to the telegram to the horticultural council to which I referred in that portion of my remarks dealing with the efforts made through Mr. Burrows to get the government to take action.

We would therefore suggest on the basis of the above brief that the anti-dumping laws be revised so as to take in all three fruits so that if there happens to be a surplus in the United States they will be prevented from dumping their surplus on the Canadian market to the detriment of the Canadian grower.
With regard to tariff, particularly tariff on apricots which is one cent per pound, we feel this is entirely inadequate. We feel that the tariff should be at least two cents a pound.

To sum up we would therefore suggest:
1.	That increased tariff protection be given to the British Columbia fruit grower.

In placing that submission before the committee and the minister it will be appreciated that I am speaking on behalf of a long established industry which is vital to the interior of the province of British Columbia. It is not a newcomer to the field; it is one of the senior primary industries of our province and they have been experiencing increasing difficulty, particularly over the past few years, with respect to this problem of the dumping of United States surplus fruits and within that field particularly the dumping of United States soft fruits.
Not too many years ago there did seem to be a considerably more flexible arrangement whereby the government of Canada could take action in the season and could apply anti-dumping provisions. My impression is that as a result to a considerable extent of the agreements made at Geneva we have lost some of the flexibility of action which we previously had. What these men are asking is that this be restored, because the people of the United States are showing very great flexibility with regard to the dumping of their surplus products. If we are going to protect our own growers in their own markets then we have to be able to take effective action to deal with these seasonal situations.
I urge upon the government both with respect to potatoes, concerning which I have not gone into detail because the details have been rehearsed here on a number of occasions previously, and also with respect to soft fruits in British Columbia, that the tariff policy be carefully reviewed and if necessary that the legislation be revised so that the effective action which is being asked for can be taken.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question. When he was comparing prices, is the price he quoted from the invoice on the United States goods with the Canadian price, the basis of his comparison, or was he comparing them with the price at which those goods were sold in the country of origin? I might state that dumping only applies when the price at which the goods were invoiced is less than the price in the country of origin. In this particular instance I would judge from what the hon. member has said that the price was comparable to the selling price in the country of origin, and therefore dumping could not be applied.

I think the minister has summarized the situation correctly, because according to the brief I have here I gather that the domestic price in the United States

Customs Tariff
virtually disappeared, and therefore they simply threw their crop on to the market and they threw it on the Canadian market at prices about 50 per cent below what had been the average price for that crop over the preceding ten years.
In the Canadian market?

Yes. The whole point being made is that if this is not defined as dumping so that no action can be taken, then we should have another look at our tariff laws and if necessary revise them in order that effective action may be taken to protect the Canadian market and Canadian growers against such a situation.
I would gather from what the minister has said that if they suddenly had a surplus in the United States or anywhere else and their domestic market disappeared-in other words if the price went down to virtually zero-they could flood our market by simply throwing the produce into it at salvage prices; and therefore, because the price for which the product was sold in Canada was not less than the price for which it was sold in the United States, I gather from what the minister says that nothing could be done about it.
We feel something should be done in such a situation in order that our markets and our growers can be protected against the fire sale prices or salvage sales of surplus products from the United States or any other country.
Your complaint is that you want the tariff raised?

My request as presented in the brief is that if the government is powerless in the light of present legislation to protect our growers from that situation, then the necessary changes should be made in the law to enable them to apply seasonal protection, whether it be called anti-dumping duties or anything else, so that our growers will not be ruined by seasonal surpluses in another country whose crop is dumped on our market.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kamloops has presented the difficulties and viewpoints of the soft tree fruit growers' and the potato growers fairly, accurately and I think in sufficient detail. However, I must explain that I had not been asked by the Progressive Conservative policy committee of Penticton to make representations in this house, but I had been asked by a number of growers in my own constituency who are seriously affected; and the points made by the hon. member for Kamloops are quite accurate.

The fruit grower and the tree fruit grower particularly is in a somewhat different position from any other type of farmer. He has a very heavy long-term investment in an orchard. When a crop becomes unproductive it is not possible for him to switch to another crop in the next year or even in two or three years. On the average he waits from 10 to 15 years for trees, depending on the variety, to come into full production, and therefore he suffers very severely if he finds himself affected, as he has been in the past two or three years, by this dumping situation that exists.
I believe the hon. member for Kamloops was quite correct; possibly under the present legislation it is not possible to do more than is being done at present. If this is so, then I think we should have another look at the legislation. I know the circumstances personally and I have spoken to a great many growers who have suffered very keenly in the last two or three years from this situation. I think further consideration should be given to an amendment to the legislation to meet this particular, and I think somewhat unusual situation.
I do ask the minister to give further consideration to the problems of these tree fruit growers and potato growers in British Columbia who have been faced in recent years with abnormal and unfair dumping on the part of the United States shippers.
May I ask another question, Mr. Speaker? Are the seasons about comparable?
We are somewhat later.
Somewhat later?
Yes, possibly two weeks on the average,
Does not the seasonal tariff meet the situation?

When the price goes down by nearly 50 per cent all the market goes down by nearly 50 per cent, and as I understand it the seasonal tariff rates are not sufficient to take care of that drastic reduction in prices.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kamloops briefly mentioned the duty that Canadian potatoes are charged when entering the United States, and he referred to the fact that United States potatoes are able to enter Canada free of duty. This is a situation which I think is completely unfair. It is a situation which is resented very strongly by the potato growers of this country, and it is something which should be righted immediately.

It is unbelievable to me that we allow United States potatoes to come into this country free, and yet the people of the United States charge a very substantial duty against Canadian potatoes. There should be equal treatment for the potatoes going into either country. Either there should be an equal duty charged or they should both enter free, and I find it unbelievable that the government has allowed a situation like this to come into existence and to continue for the length of time it has without making any apparent attempt to right a situation which is very wrong indeed.
New Brunswick potato growers have told me that potatoes from Maine cross the border free of duty, are loaded in Canadian freight cars and shipped to Montreal and Toronto under the maritime freight rates arrangement to compete with New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island potatoes on those markets. That to me is completely unfair. I should like to have assurance from the government that this completely wrong state of affairs will be righted.
I am interested in hearing the hon. member for Kootenay East make fun of a serious presentation on behalf of growers in this country who are trying to make an honest living.
I am making fun of you, not of a serious situation.
If there is anything to make fun of in an hon. member standing up and arguing the case of the growers of any product in this country, then the hon. member is justified.

speechtext:
No. I have reconciled myself to being here until Labour day, but I have not expected to go till Christmas.
In the first place, sir, everyone seems to think that trade can be a one-way street. Everyone wants the products that he has in mind kept out of Canada and he wants the products he is producing shipped into the United States; and he expects the government of Canada to induce the government of the United States to agree to that on all occasions.
Let us consider for a moment the turkeys. At the close of the war and for a good many years after that, there was an active trade with the United States for Canadian turkeys. Through that time the United States did not raise the tariff against us on turkeys; they

accepted the situation, and we developed a turkey industry in this country beyond the expectation of most people up to that time. Now the trade has turned the other way, and they would expect us to stop the trade, even if it is only temporary, for a two or three-year period, during which time there is competition in Canada for the Canadian turkey grower.
The Canadian turkey grower has not had a surplus of turkeys in any given year; he has sold every turkey he has produced in every year to which I have paid any attention. When the turkey producers see me every year they admit that they are able to sell their product, and only once have I received representations that there was some difficulty in the price, in so far as getting their costs out of the article were concerned.
However, in addition to that, there did seem to me to be some case for consideration for turkey growers, and we took it up at Geneva in the recent negotiations. I tabled in the house two months ago the result, and that result is that the tariff on turkeys going into the United States and coming into Canada is about the same. I am a little surprised to hear anyone raise the question at this late date.
With respect to the fruit growers in British Columbia, I must say that I was not aware of the discussion with my colleague this evening, but it seems to me that my colleague has correctly interpreted the statute with respect to the anti-dumping legislation and that if, as my hon. friend from Kamloops says, there is any deficiency in that law, then it would be a matter for consideration whether we should change the law. In so far as my responsibility goes, I shall have a look at the problem he has raised.
On the subject of potatoes, may I say to my hon. friend from Broadview that he seems to be labouring under the impression that he is going to succeed the late R. B. Bennett with respect to the nature of Canada's trade. That gentleman who headed the last Conservative government seemed to think that all you had to do was stand up in the House of Commons and demand tariff changes and demand that the other countries should agree to take your suggestions regardless of what their tariff might be. In 1935, after this government came into office, we renegotiated our trade arrangements with the United States, and we made particular tariff arrangements with respect to potatoes. The potato growers of Canada have enjoyed a long period of prosperity they had not experienced under the Tory government.
