Mr. Chairman, I have one or two things I should like to say on this bill. I do not want to take much time, but there are some things I think should be said about it. In the first place I want to express my satisfaction-in fact, I might go so far as to say my relief-that this bill has finally reached the floor of the House of Commons for third reading. I wish it had gone further in some aspects. I wish it had been in its original form. I think we may have unplugged one of the loopholes that was plugged in the original bill and that this may cause us trouble in the future, but I am sure the fact that it has been passed substantially in the form in which it was given second reading in the house is a matter of considerable satisfaction to most members.
But I do think, sir, that the situation that was revealed during the hearings on the bill in the banking and commerce committee is something that should receive the very greatest concern of all members of the house. I have a feeling that, while this measure will perhaps curtail at least some of the possible abuses in consumer credit operations, nevertheless the situation in that field is, I think, almost alarming.
The figures produced recently by the Bank of Canada show what the situation is. I have been putting down in short form some of the significant statistics released by the Bank of Canada in its statistical summary, and I find that consumer credit between March 31, 1955, and March 31 of this year, on selected items, increased from $1,776 million to $2,128 million, an increase of 20 per cent. At the same time and during the same period, personal savings increased only from $5,226 million to $5,865 million, an increase of only 12 per cent. Labour income during the same period increased only some 10 per cent. Net profits after taxes by corporations, however, increased 28 per cent in the same period.
I think, sir, these figures present a picture that should cause grave concern to most responsible Canadian citizens. It is quite useless for us to scold the citizens of Canada, or so many of them, who are indulging in this consumer credit spree at the present time, and tell them that they should moderate their demands on our economy and on our society. We sometimes forget, I think, that

Small Loans Act
the yardstick of what is a desirable or an acceptable standard of living is a yardstick that is constantly changing, constantly increasing in our economy; and that while we may perhaps congratulate ourselves that practically every family in Canada can, if it wishes, get enough to eat, enough to clothe itself and possibly enough living accommodation, if it is prepared, in the case of many of them, to forgo altogether all hope of having a vast variety of things held in front of their eyes seven days a week as not only desirable but as absolutely necessary if they are going to classify themselves as decent citizens at all. The consequence is that the real income of a vast number of people is no longer sufficient to meet these demands for the rising standard of living which is displayed in front of their eyes. Then we get this ballooning of consumer credit, which I think produces at the present time a very dangerous situation.
During one of the hearings of the banking and commerce committee last week a very distinguished parliamentarian from the other place pointed out to us that there are some very dangerous and sinister parallels to be drawn between this consumer credit situation today and the situation that existed in 1929, though he was careful to point out that the parallel should not be pressed too far. I do think, sir, that now that we have, as I say, plugged some of the loopholes and have placed some curbs on possible abuses, we should deal with the fundamental issue, the necessity of a vast number of Canadian citizens having access to a much larger income than they have at present. Unless they do, then this situation is going to get continually worse as our gross national product goes up by leaps and bounds, as the disparity between the percentage increase in profits, personal savings and personal incomes continues to get wider and wider, as it has done in recent years.
Just in case any member wants to console himself by thinking that measures have already been taken to cope with this situation and we are levelling off, I may say that is an entirely false impression. The last lump from March 31, 1955, to March 31 this year has been the largest jump, not only absolutely but in percentage. The matter is getting steadily worse, and this parliament will eventually have to deal with it much more fundamentally than in the bill which I have great satisfaction in supporting tonight, although as I say I wish it had been in the form in which it was originally presented to this house.

We have made considerable progress today, and I do not want to be

accused of stalling further progress so my remarks will be very brief. We all recognize that it is in the public interest to enact legislation that will protect the person who may be obliged to seek a small loan from being forced to pay an excessive amount of interest to the lender. Unfortunately the common practice of money lending has not in the past been without abuse. It should always be our aim to eliminate the unscrupulous money sharks who prey on the distress in which people sometimes find themselves. I believe, in any consideration of the problem, we should try to enact legislation that will be fair to the legitimate licensed lender in order that he may provide services which are needed, and therefore make it unnecessary for people to seek out the operator who works illegally.
I suppose it was to effect that purpose that the bill, in its original form, was sent to the banking and commerce committee. This was to allow a study of the terms of the original act and give an opportunity to make it more equitable. I was not a member of that committee from the very beginning. My membership started quite late in the hearings. Nevertheless I received some very astonishing impressions. The consumer credit of our country has reached an all-time high.
I noticed an item in Business Week of August 4, 1956, in which it is stated that personal income in the United States for June stands at $324 billion, and that 63 per cent of the United States families have debts. It seems to me that indicates very strongly that today people just have not enough money. It should be the objective of our fiscal policies to try to leave more of that purchasing dollar in the pocket of the average Canadian. Unfortunately the taxation laws of the country at present remove too much of that purchasing power. As indicated by the previous speaker the rates of interest called for in the bill will bring some relief to the small borrower. I cannot agree that they will seriously damage the business of the licensed operator.
I should like to see the chartered banks of Canada get into this field to a greater extent. While it may not be as profitable for them as other fields, I believe they ought to realize they have a great stake in the economy and well-being of the people as a whole. The availability of small loans, I believe, is a help to mass markets and the support of mass production, and it is in loans to this latter field that the banks do make substantial profits. I should like to see, therefore, some inducement given the chartered banks to operate to a greater extent in the small loans field.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I made the first part of my presentation on this subject at about a quarter to ten one evening some little time ago-I think it was July 24-I said there was only one other aspect of the bill that I wished to say anything about. It would not have occurred to me to say anything about it if it had not been for some of the observations which were made at the resolution stage in anticipation of the bill, when it was suggested, because in one or two places-as a matter of fact I have made a count of them and I think there are five-in the present bill the minister is substituted for the governor in council, that this was an attempt to make constitutional changes that might be either detrimental to the Indians or derogatory to the proper control which parliament has over the ministry.
So far as the effect on the Indians may be of any of those changes, I think hon. gentlemen would very quickly see that they all relate to very minor matters about which it is just not conceivable that the governor in council would in fact take a different view from the view taken by the minister. But because the question was also brought up in other contexts in this present session, and because it does seem to me to have some real importance for the future of our parliamentary institutions, I do want to take a very few
Indian Act
minutes to explain to the house why certain powers are transferred to the minister in this bill and why it has been done in some other bills that over the last few years have been presented to parliament.
In the first place, it does not seem to me that there is any valid argument for the proposition that there is the slightest diminution of ministerial responsibility to parliament, if a minister is empowered to do something rather than the governor in council. In fact an argument could be made that it really increases the responsibility to parliament because it identifies in inescapable fashion the person who really is responsible and the person who can be called to account. The responsibility of the governor in council is, I admit, both an individual and a collective responsibility. But the responsibility of the minister, when the power is given to the minister by parliament, is a purely individual responsibility, and nobody but the minister in question can be blamed if the action taken under the powers given to him by parliament is an action of which parliament does not approve, or of which any member of parliament does not approve. It places the responsibility, in other words, squarely on the shoulders of the minister.
This subject is not a new one. As long ago as 1912 Sir Robert Borden, one of the Canadian prime ministers for whom I have always had a great admiration and a great respect, engaged a very distinguished British civil servant, who had been at one time a private secretary to Mr. Gladstone when he was prime minister of Great Britain to make a report upon the executive government of Canada and the way in which it was carried out. There is not much doubt that a good many improvements in our executive procedure would have been carried out long ago if the first world war had not intervened and this report of Sir George Murray had not been sidetracked.
Because this report so completely justifies the course taken in this bill and in other legislation that has already been before parliament, and I hope will be found in many bills that will come before parliament in the future, I should like to read to the house the first part of the report which was made by Sir George Murray to Sir Robert Borden. He was not Sir Robert Borden then; he was Mr. Borden on November 30, 1912. The report begins in this way:
The Right Hon. R. L. Borden, K.C.,
Prime Minister.
Sir:
I have the honour to inform you, that so far as the time at my disposal will permit, I have completed the inquiry, with which you were good

Indian Act
enough to entrust me, into the organization of the public service of Canada; and X beg to submit the following report.
(2)	At the outset I may perhaps be allowed to say that no one can be more conscious than I am how- little weight any views of mine on this subject are entitled to carry, owing to the difficulty of forming a judgment on matters depending so largely on local conditions and local sentiment, the effect of which cannot be fully realized without a prolonged stay in the country. I ought, however, to add that while there are some points to which I should have been glad to give more attention if time had permitted, there are others on which I think it is unlikely that my conclusions would have been affected by further consideration.
(3)	I propose to deal with the questions referred to me in the order in which they stand in my instructions.
I.	The methods employed in the transaction of public business.
(4)	My suggestions under this head will be confined almost exclusively to the functions of ministers and the possibility of affording them relief, leaving for a later portion of the report some other questions of departmental organization.
(5)	Nothing has impressed me so much in the course of my inquiry as the almost intolerable burden which the present system of transacting business imposes on ministers themselves. They both have too much to do and do too much.
And I do not think it is any less true in 1956 than it was in 1912. I continue:
(6)	Speaking broadly, it may be said that every act of the executive government, or of any member of it, requires the sanction of the governor in council which, under present practice, is identical with the cabinet.
(7)	The number of these orders in council averages from 3,000 to 4,000 per annum,-
That was in 1912. The report continues.
-and their subject matter ranges from questions of the highest importance, such as the approval of a treaty with some foreign power, the disallowance of provincial legislation, the appointment of a judge, or the exercise of the prerogative of mercy, down to the acceptance of a tender for the erection of a pump, the promotion of a clerk from one grade to another, and the appointment of a lighthouse keeper or an excise man.
(8)	Almost every decision of a minister, even of the most trivial importance, is thus-at least in theory brought before his colleagues for the purpose of obtaining their collective approval, which is necessary for its validity.
(9)	Provisions to this effect can be traced in almost every act of parliament which has been passed since confederation; and it seems clear that the statesmen of that time thought it necessary to ensure that the collective responsibility of the cabinet for the action of individual ministers should be protected by safeguards of this kind.
(10)	But I need scarcely point out that a great deal has happened since 1867-
And I might add a great deal more has han-pened since 1912.
-and the methods of administration which may have been well adapted to the circumstances of those days have become quite unsuitable after the lapse of nearly half a century.
And that half century has now grown to 89 years.
(11)	With the increase of population, the extension of trade, and the development of the

various activities of the state, the business of government necessarily grows both in amount and in complexity.
(12)	The only means by which this growth can be met is by division of labour and devolution of power. In the absence of some continuous process of this kind the machinery of government must gradually become less efficient and must ultimately break down under the stress imposed upon it.
(13)	Many topics which, in the early stages of national life, may properly form the subject of collective discussion and decision, will in the course of time diminish in relative importance, and must be dealt with in some more summary fashion.
Before reading the next paragraph I might remind hon. members that this was written in 1912. I continue:
(14)	The first suggestion which I have to offer is that many of the powers now vested in the governor in council should, by some process of devolution, be transferred to individual ministers. At times mistakes will no doubt be made.
Of course this was written in 1912.

It would I think be generally conceded that a minister should be able to give leave of absence to the officers of his department; to grant statutory increases of salary; to sanction the acceptance of tenders, except where very large amounts or questions of principle are involved; to make appointments to vacancies; and to promote the clerks in his department from one class to another.
I only mention these as illustrations of the general character of the changes proposed. There are many others which will readily occur to any one who will examine the details of the existing system.
Now, sir, there have been a few useful changes made in recent years. The most important of these changes, I think, was the passing by this parliament of the Financial Administration Act, which did provide that many of the functions which were formerly performed by the governor in council and which imposed an utterly intolerable burden of purely routine work upon-not really the whole cabinet after the beginning of the war of 1939, but upon a large number of ministers-could	be discharged by the
treasury board and in many cases could be discharged by a very small committee of the treasury board.
What the effect of that change has been can be illustrated when I remind hon. members of what they no doubt know already; that in the year 1951 there were 6,874 orders in council passed in Canada and 10,066 orders of the treasury board, and in the year 1955 there were 1,847 orders in council and 2,116 minutes of the treasury board.
This does not mean that the government did less business in 1955 than in 1951. It does mean, however, that the work was done with a great deal more efficiency because of an enactment of this parliament about which I think there was very little controversy.
When one comes to look at the difference between the practice in Canada and the practice in the United Kingdom it is evident that we still require the governor in council to do an enormous amount of work which in the United Kingdom is entrusted to individual ministers. I had a look at the statistics for the United Kingdom for the
Indian Act
year 1954, the last year for which figures are available here, and they had 1,761 statutory instruments which were issued in the year 1954. Of that total of 1,761 there were 102 orders in council, of which 38 related to colonial matters. In other words out of a total of 1,761 much less than 10 per cent were orders in council.
In 1954 we in Canada had 705 statutory orders and regulations, a considerably smaller number than the British had, though hon. gentlemen opposite are always fond of talking about our having government by order in council in Canada. Of our 705 statutory orders and regulations 478 were orders in council, and I think that number is still too great.
I believe it would be very desirable if we could go on and make more progress along the road that Sir George Murray pointed out to the Borden government in 1912, and the very modest step in this direction in the present bill is one that I am not in the least ashamed of because I think it is moving in the right direction.

subtopic: C. B. C., VANCOUVER-LEGAL ADVISERS
C. B. C., VANCOUVER-LEGAL ADVISERS
speechtext:
What are the names and addresses of the legal advisers to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the city of Vancouver, British Columbia?
Answer by: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation advises as follows:
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation employs or retains no legal advisers in Vancouver, British Columbia, but has, on occasion, in Vancouver as elsewhere, engaged the services of different legal Arms for assistance in the conduct of its business.

subtopic: USE OF FLAG ON MAY 25
USE OF FLAG ON MAY 25
speechtext:
1. Has the Minister of Public Works concluded the investigation in connection with the ownership of the flag used by the hon. member for
Questions
Hamilton West to drape the desk of the hon. member for Eglinton in the House of Commons on the afternoon of May 25 last?
2.	If so, whose property was the flag?
3.	By whom, and for what purpose was it requested, and from whom was it obtained?
4.	Was the request for the flag made previous to 4 p.m. of May 25? If so, at what time?
5.	Has the flag been returned to its owner, and, if so, when?
Answer by:	Mr. Bourgei, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Public Works:
1.	Yes.
2.	The red ensign was the property of the House of Commons.
3.	It was requested by the office of the Leader of the Opposition for a "party". The flag was obtained from the assistant chief of equipment and purchaser, House of Commons.
4.	The request for the flag was made at 12.20 p.m. (noon), Friday, May 25, 1956. It was delivered to the office of the Leader of the Opposition at 1 p.m. on the same day.
5.	The assistant chief of equipment and purchaser went to the office of the Leader of the Opposition at 9.30 a.m., May 28, 1956, and recovered the flag.
